en: *The Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Ming*, Volume One,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Ruxing of Ciyun Chan Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Hongwu era.

Section One: Translation of Scriptures Chapter One: Biographies of Translators The Biography of the Śramaṇa Śālaripa of Qingshou Monastery in the Yuan Capital Yan; with two supplementary accounts. The Biography of the Śramaṇa Śālaripa of Qingshou Monastery in the Yuan Capital Yan. Śālaripa (also known as Chos-rje-dpal) was a native of Jining in the western region of Sogdiana. He was a descendant of the royal lineage of the Qarluq Turks. His father was named Bulga Rasipā. At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under the master Sengge. He studied the *Vinaya* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, and also mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. He traveled extensively throughout India, where he encountered the great master of the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*, the venerable Dharmapāla. He received from him the instructions on the *Cakrasaṃvara-mahātantrarāja* and other teachings. He also studied the *Hevajra-tantra* under the master Vajraghaṇṭa. Having mastered these, he returned to his own country. Later, he traveled to China during the reign of Emperor Shizu (Kublai Khan). He translated the *Mahāmāyā-tantra* and other works. He resided at Qingshou Monastery in the capital, where he passed away at the age of seventy-four. He was posthumously honored with the title "National Preceptor of Great Virtue" (*Guoshi Dade*). His disciple, the Śramaṇa Chos-kyi-grags-pa, succeeded him. Supplementary Account One: The Śramaṇa Chos-kyi-grags-pa was a native of the western regions. He traveled to China during the reign of Emperor Chengzong and resided at Qingshou Monastery. He translated the *Vajrabhairava-tantra* and other texts. He passed away at the age of sixty-six. Supplementary Account Two: The Śramaṇa Blo-gros-rgyal-mtshan was a native of the western regions. He traveled to China during the reign of Emperor Renzong and resided at Qingshou Monastery. He translated the *Amoghapāśa-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* and other works. He passed away at the age of fifty-nine. (Note: The original text contains the transliterated name "Shaluo ba" [Śālaripa] and identifies him as a person from the Western Regions, specifically Jining, with the title "Śramaṇa" and the monastery "Qingshou" in the Yuan capital Yan.)
In his youth, he received the tonsure under the master Ras-pa-sde and studied the initiation rituals of the various tantra classes.
Furthermore, he studied both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna under the master Zhag-ri-khri.
At that time, there was a person named Ratnabhadra who was highly proficient in the Yamāntaka secret teachings and was renowned throughout the world for his mastery of them.
He applied himself until he had mastered the Way.
Thus, he was adept at pronouncing Tibetan sounds and expounding the various sublime Dharmas, while simultaneously understanding the scripts of many nations.
Later, Garu Sibadi (Karma Pakshi) recommended him to the Great Ancestor (Shizu).
He ordered the translation of various scriptures of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings not yet prepared in China,
totaling several tens of thousands of fascicles;
their wording and meaning were clear and lucid.
He was specially granted the title "Great Eloquence and Vast Wisdom.
At that time, although the monastic administration was flourishing, its discipline and integrity had fallen into decay;
thus, the officials were unable to serve as a bulwark for the bequeathed Dharma to resist external provocations.
On the contrary, they were harmed by the monastic community.
Whenever Emperor Shizu discussed this matter, he was deeply concerned.
He therefore selected capable individuals to rectify these failings and restore order.
Therefore, he was specially appointed as the General Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings for Jiangzhe and other regions.
The Emperor personally saw him off with words of encouragement.
Upon arriving in Jiangnan, he abolished all cumbersome and oppressive regulations and devoted himself to policies of broad leniency.
Consequently, monasteries both far and near relied upon him for their security.
He subsequently changed his name to Tongfuguang;
because of the Master’s upright spirit, his virtue was majestic and solemn, lofty and independent.
Consequently, he frequently clashed with his colleagues.
He once sighed to himself, saying,
"What is this world for?"
It is we ourselves who disturb it.
The more officials the court appoints,
the more complex the affairs of the empire become.
How much more so for the teachings of Śākyamuni!
The current hardships faced by the monastic community have no other cause;
they stem simply from the excessive demands and bureaucratic complexities of the government.
As the saying goes, "ten sheep with nine shepherds"—how can this be described?
He subsequently submitted a memorial to report this matter.
Having received imperial approval, he abolished the positions of Regional Commissioners (zongtong) across all circuits.
The whole world rejoiced in this.
The Master then withdrew from public view to a hillock,
where he built a dwelling and planted trees, intending to spend his final years there.
During the Zhizhidao era, he was summoned once again to Yanjing (Beijing),
where he was appointed as a Minister of Rites (Dàsītú) and a Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglùdàfū).
The Crown Prince and various princes frequently consulted him on the essentials of the Dharma.
By imperial decree, he was granted provisions and lodging at Qingshou Temple.
All the scriptures he translated were published by the court.
On the fifth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Yanʼyou era, he manifested illness.
He was granted ten thousand strings of cash.
The Imperial Edict commanded Prince Shen, the Grand Marshal, to attend to his medical needs, but he declined them;
in the end, he sat upright facing the Buddha and passed away.
The Emperor, lamenting his loss with deep sorrow, granted him a state funeral and dispatched an envoy on an express courier to escort his remains back to his native village.
A stupa was erected there. The postscript says:
The flourishing of scripture translation was unsurpassed during the Six Dynasties and the High Tang, with figures such as Kumārajīva and Śikṣānanda at its zenith.
Upon entering the Five Dynasties and the Northern Song, however, it gradually declined.
How much more so since the time Emperor Kang crossed the river and the Hu horses drank from the south;
the imperial carriage fled in haste, and even after the Chunxi era,
though there was a brief interval of leisure.
How could such a thing have been possible?
It was not until the reign of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty that China and the non-Chinese were unified under one rule,
and only then was the imperial decree issued once more for the translation of Buddhist scriptures.
Since the founding of our dynasty in the first year of the Hongwu era,
because the Tripitaka was largely complete and Dharmaratna did not arrive, this precedent alone has been followed.
Thus, in the *History of Yuan*, we find only this one individual.
I hope that this first category will not be in vain; it is indeed rare indeed. **Section Two:

Explication of Meaning (Jièyìpiān), Part One.** **Section Two: Explication of Meaning, Part One.** **The Main Biographies: Thirty-nine Persons; Nine Persons Seen in Appendix.** 1. **Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Jingzhen of Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang.** Regarding the Śramaṇa Shi Jingzhen of Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang: his family name and origins are unknown.
He received the tonsure and studied the Xianshou school under Dharma Master Ruoping at Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang.
In the third year of the Jiaxi era, he traveled to various monasteries throughout Zhejiang;
at that time, the dykes of the Qiantang River had collapsed, causing the river tides to overflow and bringing disaster upon the people.
The Master presented a verse to Zhao Duanming, the Pacification Commissioner, saying:
"The seas boil and the rivers flow in continuous succession;
the dwellings of the people are swept away, increasing their anguish."
He cast himself directly into the dragon palace;
wishing to stop the surging waves that struck the heavens, he threw himself into the sea and returned after three days.
He said to the residents:
"I shall preach the Dharma in the Dragon Palace, and the dragon deities shall listen and receive it.
This pond shall never again be destroyed.
Having finished speaking, he once more cast himself into the sea.
Zhao Duoming, moved by his virtue, reported the matter in full to the court.
By imperial decree, he was bestowed the title of State Preceptor Jingzhen (Huguo Jingzhen Fashi),
and a shrine was established for him at Huicisi in Hangzhou.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zujué of Zhongyan Temple in Meizhou, Part Two. The Śramaṇa Shi Zujué of Zhongyan Temple in Meizhou was also known by the sobriquet Chian (The Hall of Folly).
He was a member of the Yang family from Jiazhou.
Intelligent and precocious from his youth, he took a singular delight in the Buddha-vehicle.
He investigated the tenets of the Xianshou school with great precision, fully mastering all their profound mysteries.
Later, by imperial decree, he went to reside at Zhongyan in Meizhou.
Scholars from all quarters arrived like clouds gathering and rivers flowing;
every day he presided over the opening of the hall, tirelessly instructing and exhorting them.
In guiding and uplifting later students, he exhausted every means of compassion;
thus, the Qingliang school reached its peak of prosperity during his tenure.
Furthermore, beyond the striking of the mallet...
He thoroughly researched all books, histories, and the classics and statutes of the various schools of thought from antiquity to the present.
He could recite them from memory upon a single reading.

He once compiled the *History of Northern Song Monks*, as well as the *Collected Explanations of the Avatamsaka Sutra*, the *Commentary on the Diamond Sutra*, and the *Ritual for the Water and Land Feast*.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Ruone of Shang Tianzhu, Lin’an. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Ruone of Shang Tianzhu, Lin’an, Part Three. Shi Ruone was appointed by imperial decree to reside at Shang Tianzhu.
He constantly led a thousand disciples and widely propagated the Way of the Three Contemplations, the Ten Vehicles, the Five Stages, and the Six Identities.
His eloquence was like a cascading torrent from a mountain spring.
He was truly one of the four reliances of the age.
In the third year of the Chunxi era of the Southern Song, Emperor Gaozong visited Shangzhu Temple wishing to pay homage to the Great Being (Bodhisattva).
Nan greeted him there.
Gaozong asked,
"In relation to the Great Being, should I prostrate or not?
Neng replied:
"If they do not bow, each will claim superiority;
if they bow, they will show mutual respect. Gaozong joyfully performed the prostration.
He then asked, "What is the purpose of the annual performance of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual?"
Nan said: "In the past,
the Buddha preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-samādhi* for Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings,
entrusting them with the protection of the nation and its people."
Later, the Patriarchs established this as a rite of repentance,
commanding that monks perform this method every New Year to pray for the blessing of the nation.
This is a ritual of a flourishing era.
The Emperor previously conferred upon Nuo the title of Right Street Monk Recorder (Youjie Senglü) and granted him funds to cultivate his Way.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, he summoned Nuo.
He led fifty monks into the Inner Meditation Hall to practice the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* Samādhi for the protection of the state.
After the meal was served and finished, Banot ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
The Emperor asked:
“The Buddha-dharma is indeed wondrous.
How could there be such a vast number of scriptures?
Nan replied:
The original text was thus.
Emperor Gaozong was greatly pleased and promoted Dao-ne to the position of Left Street Monk Registrar,
bestowing upon him the title Master Huiguang.
From then on, every year on this day, he would enter the palace to perform Buddhist rites.
He was granted fifty rolls of silk.

In the eighth month of the seventh year, he summoned Neng to the palace to bestow a vegetarian feast and preach the Dharma; his teachings met with the Emperor's approval, and the imperial favor bestowed upon him was exceptionally profound and extraordinary.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Liao Ran of Bailian Temple in Taizhou, Part IV. The śramaṇa Shi Liao Ran, whose style name was Zhiyong, [was a native of] Taizhou.
He left the household life at Baolian Temple in Jun County and lectured on the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai for over twenty years.
He diligently encouraged his later disciples, while he himself cultivated pure karma in private.
He took but one meal a day and remained seated in meditation until dawn.
One night he dreamed that two dragons were sporting amidst the clouds in the expanse of space; suddenly, they transformed into divine beings.
Descending from the sky, he came to visit the Master. Then,
producing a letter from his sleeve, he showed it to him, saying,
"Seven days from now, you shall depart for the West."
Having clearly awakened from his trance, Liaoran realized it was a response signaling his rebirth in the Pure Land.
He then beat the drum to assemble the congregation,
ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, and gave instructions regarding his final affairs.
Thereafter, he wrote a verse, saying:
"By relying on the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, one attains birth in the Land of Bliss.
You all, therefore, should not be indolent."
He immediately requested a bath and changed his robes.
He then instructed the assembly to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* in unison.
Upon reaching the passage concerning the Western World, he suddenly passed away.
The entire assembly heard the sound of celestial music filling the air, and auspicious light illuminated the heavens. 5.

Śramaṇa Shi Liaoxuan of Baolin Monastery in Mingzhou, a native of Siming, propagated the Five Virtues that Bring Prosperity. Śramaṇa Shi Liaoxuan of Baolin Monastery in Mingzhou, a native of Siming, propagated the Five Virtues that Bring Prosperity.
He pursued his studies at Baolin Monastery;
subsequently, admiring the flourishing reputation of Nanhu,
he joined it there and devoted himself to a thorough investigation of the principles of the Three Contemplations and the Ten Vehicles.
Having perused the Tripitaka, there was no great meaning he did not understand.
He practiced the Lotus Repentance Ritual for twenty-seven years and was on excellent terms with his fellow practitioner, Shi Shanrong.

In all his spiritual cultivation and advancement, he invariably shared in its glory, having personally transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Śūraṃgama-samādhi*, *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and *Yuanjue* (Awakening of Faith) sutras in golden script;
Xuan also assisted him in these efforts.
Whenever he encountered a memorial service for his deceased parents (*xīzī huì*), he would bestow upon others hand-painted ink-and-water images of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
The two of them made a vow to be reborn together.
Whenever they preached the Dharma, they earnestly exhorted others to seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Many followed their example and practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name.
One day, Xuán went to Róng’s residence and sat in silence.
Róng intentionally questioned him,
and he replied:
"I am about to return to the West; I can hardly forget our shared path of righteousness.
May we meet again in the Pure Land.
Yong said:
In accordance with his sincere aspirations,
Xuān immediately assembled the congregation to bid him farewell,
commanding them to recite the sutras and chant the Buddha’s name.
Sitting upright, he wrote a verse, saying:
"Nature and form are forgotten;
in oneness and threefoldness there is no reliance."
His breath ceased and his vital winds no longer moved;
Mahāśrī joined his palms and passed away during the height of the summer heat.
The reliquary chamber remained closed for seven days.
His complexion was ruddy and moist, and there was a slight trace of saliva at the corners of his mouth.
When onlookers wiped it away with a cloth, a wondrous fragrance wafted toward them.
The city’s elite and commoners flocked there, their fragrant saliva increasing its moisture.
After his cremation, the śarīra relics were beyond counting.
Three years passed since he entered nirvana.
Rong suddenly took the scriptures and images and distributed them among his relatives and acquaintances;
he had them recite the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra* and the *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra*,
and led the assembly to assist him in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Sitting in the full lotus posture, he said,
"I am going to fulfill my promise to Master Xuan.
Having finished speaking, his body suddenly transformed and vanished.

6. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xingcheng of Shang Tianzhu, Hangzhou, Yuan Dynasty Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xingcheng of Shang Tianzhu, Hangzhou, Yuan Dynasty, Number Six. Shi Xingcheng, a monk from Yunmengze, whose courtesy name was Zhantang and sobriquet Yuexi.
He was the son of the Sun family of Kuaiji in Shaoxing.
His father was Man and his mother was Lady Jiang.
She dreamed that a solar disc fell from the sky.
Upon waking, he found that the sunlight was still shining upon his bed, whereupon he conceived the aspiration for the Teacher [the Buddha].
At the age of four, he would often playfully take up a brush to paint images of the Buddha;
when given Buddhist scriptures, he could recite them from memory as if they were the result of past habituation.
In the *bingzi* year of the Yuan Zhiyuan era, Master Shu of Shimen tonsured his head and received full ordination.
Shimen said, "The precepts are the root of all Buddhas of the three periods; therefore, one must investigate the Vinaya-piṭaka. Thus, he delved into the Vinaya collection.
He thoroughly mastered the meanings of the dual and single prohibitions, as well as the principles of cessation, maintenance, action, and transgression.
In the year of Yiyou (1605), he studied the Tiantai teachings and contemplations under Master Fojian Xian;
subsequently, he visited Dharma Master Yunmeng Ze at Pufu Temple in Nan Zhu.
Zé (Zhao Zongben) saw him at once and held him in high esteem.
He successively occupied various prestigious and important posts.
Because Tiantai Guoqing Temple was originally a lecture monastery of the Tiantai school that had later been converted into a Chan monastery, [he was appointed there].
He then traveled several thousand li to the capital and submitted a detailed memorial regarding the origins and history of the temple’s establishment, as well as the basis for its former regulations.
Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty granted him an imperial edict in seal-script to restore them.
Subsequently, he wished to cross the Yalu River to the east to travel through Goryeo in search of the lost texts of Tiantai;
however, hearing that his country was in a state of turmoil, he abandoned the plan.

In the year Daye (1305), he went forth to reside at Dongzhu in Hangzhou. In the year Dingwei (1307), Wuyue suffered a great drought; the Master led the assembly in preaching the Dharma and praying for rain, which was answered with such efficacy that the people, suffering from famine and dying, had no means to provide coffins for burial.
He then performed a great water and land assembly (*shuilu dahui*) to enshroud his remains and universally deliver them.
In the year Daming Wushen, he was moved to Yanfu Monastery in Southern India (Nan-zhu).
In the year Zhizhi Xinyou, he was summoned by imperial decree to the capital.
He sought instruction in the Way at Myeonginjeon Hall.
By imperial decree, he resided at Cheongtasa Temple to collate the Tripitaka.
When the Emperor visited Munsugak Pavilion, he was summoned for an audience, where the Emperor greeted him with kind inquiries.
He was granted several volumes each of such scriptures as the *Sūtra of Amitāyus*.
Upon the completion of his mission and his formal leave to return, he was specially bestowed with a gold-embroidered robe (*jinalan yi*).
Just as he was about to depart, an imperial decree arrived ordering that a great *shuilu* (water-land) *mochie* (unrestricted) assembly be established immediately at Bailian Temple.
At that time, the Chancellor, Prince Zhongxian of Dongping, requested that he ascend the seat to preach the Dharma.
When this matter was reported to the Emperor, the imperial favors bestowed upon him were especially abundant;
he was granted the honorary title of Great Master Fohai.
In the Jiazi year of the Taiding era, he resided at Upper Tianzhu for nine years.
On the first day of the sixth month in the Renshen year of the Zhishun era, he suddenly beat the drum and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have occupied this famous mountain for over thirty years."
My own practice has been of no benefit and worldly conditions are limited;
though I am ashamed of my lack of talent, the noble spirit of the ancient masters may still be emulated.
Ultimately, I shook out my robes and returned to the clouds beyond India, to the Zhai hermitage.
After more than a year, he returned to Fuguo in Yue.
He devoted himself earnestly to the Pure Land, practicing the threefold contemplation with single-minded focus for seven days and nights,
frequently experiencing auspicious responses.
One day at dawn, when the assembly was making their customary inquiries,
the Master hurriedly bowed and said,
"If it were not for my urgent need to take a step back, I would not have done so."
Twelve years have already passed, with more than half gone.
Today may come, but tomorrow is uncertain.
How can one afford to toy with the passage of time?
He requested that his robes and bowl be displayed for a short time to manifest impermanence,
and the assembly recited the Buddha’s name for him.
He then said, "Stop."
The Buddha thought to himself,
"I shall see him off tomorrow morning.
At dawn, as the assembly gathered, he sat upright and passed away.
He lived for seventy-eight years and sat in meditation for sixty-four summer retreats.
His remains were kept in the shrine for seven days, his countenance appearing as if alive.
His entire body was interred in the Qingtai Pagoda Courtyard.

Among his writings are the *Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra*, the *Annotated Sections of the Heart Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Sūtra for the Elimination of Calamities*, the *Phrase-by-Phrase Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra*, as well as the *Sectional Outline of the Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and the *Sectional Outline of the Ruyilun Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Circulating in the world. 7.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Mengrun of Xiazhu Temple in Hangzhou. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Mengrun of Xiazhu Temple in Hangzhou, Number Seven. [The lineage] of Gu Yuan Zhutang transmits that the Śramaṇa Shi Mengrun, whose courtesy name was Yugang, [was...]
He was a native of Haiyan in Jiahe.
His surname was Gu,
and his father, Min, was a recluse.
His mother, née Sun, was the niece of the Dharma Master Guoyuan Qing.
During her pregnancy and at the time of his birth, she experienced extraordinary dreams.
When Zhiren was fourteen years old, he entered the service of Guoyuan at Bailian in the prefecture.
When he was about to pay homage to the shrine deity of the monastery, all the earthen statues toppled over;
the entire assembly was struck with wonder.
Whenever Gu Yuan was taught a scripture, he would immediately master it through recitation.
He then ordered that [the Master] follow Master Xiang to have his hair shaved and receive full ordination.
Upon seeing his keen intelligence, Gu Yuan instructed him in various texts, including the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the *Jingangbei*, and the *Shier Buermen*.
He was immediately able to grasp the great meaning;
having realized the ancient source and returned to stillness, he served Master Chuan at Zhutang to complete his studies.
Due to his arduous studies, he contracted a strange illness.
He practiced the Repentance Ritual for Invoking Avalokiteśvara for seven seven-day periods.
Having obtained a miraculous response, his illness was swiftly cured,
and his mind became twice as clear and sharp.
Consequently, he obtained a seat at Yanfu Monastery in Southern India;
when Master Tanzhang Cheng arrived to preside over the abbacy,
Zhirun occupied the first seat.
In the summer, Wuhe Chushiu lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* at Dezang Monastery in Danghu, Haiyan;
the assembly often numbered in the thousands, including even butchers and wine-sellers.
He changed his occupation for their sake;
the traces of his auspicious responses are beyond counting.
As he moved on, the tradition of the lineage of merit flourished even more vibrantly.
Regarding his departure from the monastery after six years:
he resided at the White Lotus Hermitage on Fenghuang Ridge by Longjing Lake,
where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *nien-fo* samādhi.
His followers increased day by day.
The Xuanzheng Yuan and those below it forcibly summoned him from his Dharma seat in India.
At that time, the temple was in the midst of a disaster.
Only the Puxian Hall stood loftily amidst brambles and rubble; thereupon,
he sighed with emotion and said to the assembly,
"This temple was established by Ciyun."
Since the Hall still stands today, the vow-power of the Founding Master remains present.
He therefore renovated it in successive stages, making it new.
Morning and evening he expounded the teachings without weariness, leading the assembly to practice the Lotus Samādhi.
He perceived the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra emitting light and manifesting various auspicious signs.
While residing at Sanjue,
one day he summoned his disciples Shimin, Hōmyō, Saiku, and others, and instructed them on the principles of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the settling of the mind (*anxin*).

After a while, he said, "The conditions for my life have nearly exhausted; now is precisely the time. He suddenly recited the Buddha's name several hundred times and then passed away in serene stillness.
Throughout his life, Run exerted himself with diligence day and night without slackening.
He once practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* on seven occasions,
each time setting a period of ninety days as his limit.
He practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the Great Compassion, and the Pure Land.
As for the period of seven times seven days, it cannot be measured by fixed numbers;
therefore, his hidden virtues, secret practices, and secret realizations are not easily fathomed by the superficial.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zhenjing of Shang Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou, Part Eight. The Śramaṇa Shi Zhenjing, whose courtesy name was Ru’an, was a person of boundless virtue. His secular surname was Chen, and he was a native of Lin’an. From childhood, his disposition was pure and his character upright; he possessed a profound and penetrating intelligence. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order under Master Zhongxian of Xiangfu Monastery in Lin’an. He received the full precepts at the age of twenty and diligently applied himself to the study of the Vinaya. Subsequently, he traveled to various regions to seek out the teachings of the Dharma. He visited the masters of the Chan school at Mount Tiantai, Mount Wutai, and Mount Jingci, as well as the great teachers of the Huayan and Tiantai schools. Having thoroughly investigated their doctrines, he returned to reside at Shang Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou. There, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of meditation and the cultivation of wisdom, never ceasing for even a moment. His spiritual power was such that it could move the heavens and earth; his miraculous responses were manifest and beyond measure. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he was summoned to the capital to preside over the ordination platform. Later, he retired to the mountains to dwell in seclusion. In the first year of the Yongxi era, he was invited by imperial decree to serve as the abbot of the Great Bao’en Monastery in the Southern Capital. He subsequently resided at the Guangzhai Monastery in the Northern Capital. In the third year of the Jiayou era, he was again summoned to the capital to preside over the ordination platform at the Kaiyuan Monastery. In the second year of the Zhenghe era, he was appointed as the Chief Preceptor of the State. In the first year of the Chunyou era, he was granted the title of "Great Master of Universal Wisdom" (Puzhi Dashi). In the fourth year of the Chunyou era, he passed away at the Shang Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou at the age of eighty-four. He had been a monk for sixty-two years. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title "Great Master of Pure Conduct" (Jingxing Dashi) and the honorific name "Virtuous and Pure. His remains were interred at the monastery. He authored several works, including the *Commentary on the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Bhadracarī Praṇidhāna*, the *Commentary on the Ten Stages Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the He left home to become a monk under the Venerable Shuntian Man at Baoji Temple in his hometown.
Even as a young child, his brilliance was peerless;
when Man gave him the Lotus Sūtra, he immediately mastered it by heart.
At the age of sixteen, he became a *bhikṣu*.
Daily he upheld the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*,
never daring to transgress its rules even by the width of a hair or the length of a ruler during his every step.
Thereafter, he sighed and said:
"The precepts must certainly not be treated with laxity;
yet one must also thoroughly investigate the Mahāyāna scriptures to support both practice and understanding."
He thought, "Could it be that I am still behind?
Thereupon, he went to Yinzhou to rely on Master Quan of Bāngshān to study the Tiantai teachings.
After a long time, he thoroughly mastered their essential principles.
He once practiced the repentance rites of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*,
and the Pure Land sutras. One day, while in meditative concentration, he had a vision of the Venerable Siming,
who entrusted him with a rhinoceros-horn *cāmara*.
From then on, his eloquence overflowed daily like a river or a cascading spring;
it flowed forth without the slightest hesitation.
In the first year of the Yuantai ding era, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Wanshou Yuanjue Monastery.
The following year, the coastline at Yanguan was destroyed.
The residents were filled with apprehension morning and evening, fearing they would become the abode of fish and turtles.
Prime Minister Yuan Tuo-huan was deeply concerned about this.
He then offered prayers to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara at Upper Zhushan.
He commanded Ji to immediately establish a great Water and Land Assembly (shuilu daqi) by the seashore and enter the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind.
Taking sand from the sea, he recited the Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī.
The commander led his troops to scatter [the earth] everywhere over that place;
wherever their footprints reached, the banks were restored to their former solidity.
People praised him as a divine being.
During the Tianli era, he moved to Xianci Temple in Jiqing;
as the year was marked by famine, he withdrew to a separate chamber.
The people of Suzhou invited him to serve as the Abbot of Wanshou Temple.
After six years of winter and summer, the temple was completed.
In the fifth year of the Zhizheng era, he was invited by the Xuanzheng Yuan to preside over Yuantong Monastery in Kuaiji,
where he resided for four years.
He returned to Baoji to single-mindedly cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation.
At the age of seventy-seven, he saved [beings] until he reached eighty.
Emperor Yuan issued an imperial decree appointing him as the abbot of Pufu Monastery in Hangzhou.
Ji lay firm in his recumbent posture and did not rise.
His disciples, including Fahang, stepped forward and said,
"It is truly excellent that the Master himself maintains such steadfastness."
"What can be done with such a path?
Constrained by necessity, he was eventually compelled to rise and accept the imperial summons;
however, before long, he ultimately shook out his robes and returned once more to his former seclusion.
He established Qingjing Ge (The Hall of the Clear Mirror) as his retreat.
Because the various commentaries on the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* were inconsistent in their degree of detail and appropriateness,
he intended to synthesize their teachings and compose a sub-commentary (*śu*).
Suddenly, his illness flared up, and he immediately summoned his disciples.
With great earnestness, he exhorted them with the principle of the Pure Land of the Mind-Only.
There were some who did not yet understand his meaning, whereupon Jì said in a stern voice:
"Difficult is the realm of birth and death; difficult is the realm of birth and death.
Having thus written this verse, he passed away.
This was on the tenth day of the third month in the sixteenth year of the Zhizheng era.
He had lived through eighty-six years of the world and had spent seventy-one summer retreats in meditation.
Seven days after his passing, his countenance remained as if he were alive.
The assembly interred him in an earthenware vessel at Songhuawu on Mount Emei in their village;
this was also the site where he had previously chosen his own burial.
His five dharma-heir disciples were Daozhen of Shangzhu, Jingchen of Yongxi, Yunchong of Puguang, Youchuan of Yuantong, and Mingjing of Tiangong.
His works include the *Sijiao yi* (Outline of the Four Teachings), the *Ji zheng tian'an waiji* (Supplementary Collection on Rectifying the Heavenly Shore), and others, totaling several volumes,
which circulate in the world.
The postscript says:
Ji possessed three qualities that surpassed those of ordinary men.
First, he could never forget anything from the inner and outer classics and histories after reading them once throughout his life.
There was a monk from Gaochang named Prajñāśrī.
Second, when I requested that he— whose learning in both Chinese and Sanskrit was unrivaled in the world—
translate the *Shorter Śamatha-vipaśyanā* using the Gaochang language,
I suddenly beheld its literary brilliance shining forth, and my mind was struck with such awe that I felt utterly lost in self-consciousness.
Throughout his life, he took it as his personal mission to propagate the teachings of the Dharma.
He preached the Lotus Sūtra on one hundred and ten occasions,
and on several instances, he was moved by the descent of celestial rain and the scattering of profuse jeweled flowers.
Alas! Among people, some may possess one of these qualities and feel no shame in their lives;
yet to be fully endowed with all three of these can truly be called the world’s *udumbara* flower.

3. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Benwu of Yanqing Temple in Siming. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Benwu of Yanqing Temple in Siming. Third: Shi Benwu, whose style name was Woaan, was a native of Huangyan, Taizhou.
In his youth, he followed Chan Master Fangshan Bao at Ruiyan to shave his head and receive full ordination.
Subsequently, he relied upon Chan Master Jizhao at Zhongtianzhu, where he was appointed to serve as the secretary for correspondence.
Jizhao frequently received profound prodding and guidance from him, through which he attained moments of realization.
Later, there was his maternal uncle,
who had originally studied the Tiantai teachings.
He escorted him to change his robes.

Seeing that Zhantang Cheng was at Yanfu Temple deeply studying the scriptural divisions (*śāstra*), Jizhao lamented his departure and composed a verse to send to him, saying: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
Entering Chan through the teachings has existed from ancient times to the present;
entering the teachings through Chan has never existed from ancient times to the present.
Although the gateways of the single mind and the three contemplations differ, [they ultimately converge].
When the waters fill a thousand rivers, the moon remains solitary.
After the Master entered the world, he became the Dharma heir of Master Cheng;
he then burned a single incense stick to repay his debt of gratitude to Jizhao.
This was because he did not allow their differing outward traces to create a duality in his mind.
When Jizhao was about to enter nirvana, while his master was presiding over Yanqing Monastery,
Jizhao left a letter entrusting him with the vigorous propagation of the two schools of Dashi and Shaolin.
There was no one else to speak of.
Because of this, Master [Zhao] Dianjiao took up the incense and said:
"The fifth transmission of Miaoxi is the most radiant flame."
The gate of ambrosia throughout this lifetime of stillness and illumination—
casually touching it, one's liver and gall burst open;
ice and snow suddenly become the warmth of spring.
I contemplate the day my nostrils were lost; what kind of breath remains even now?
The celestial wind comes from the north as the year draws to a close;
a flash of lightning seeks out the traces in the void.
Later in his life, the Master resided at Upper Tianzhu in Hangzhou for the longest period.
One day, without illness, he sat upright and passed away in the Baiyun Hall.
He was posthumously titled Great Master Fohu Xuanjue Xianci Kuangdao.

4. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xingkē of Xiuchan Temple on Mount Fulong at Tiantai. The biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xingkē of Xiuchan Temple on Mount Fulong at Tiantai, number four. The Śramaṇa Shi Xingkē was styled Yixing.
He comprehensively mastered the Tiantai school and diligently cultivated *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).
His practice was grounded in reality and his realization of principle was perfectly integrated.
One night, while listening to the rain, he composed a verse, saying:
Drops falling before the eaves are most distinct;
sentient beings in their delusion call them sounds.
I too, in recent years, have often pursued external objects.
On a spring night, a single pillow made it difficult for him to form a dream.
It is not known how his life ended. 5.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Wencai of Youguo Monastery on Mount Wutai. Shi Wencai, whose courtesy name was Zhonghua, was a native of Jiaoluo. He was a śramaṇa at Youguo Monastery on Mount Wutai.
He was the son of Lady Yang of Qing-shui.
His ancestors were from Hong-nong, where generations of officials served at Long-di.
His father, Jing-yi, served as the Magistrate’s Assistant (Zhu-bu) of Qing-shui and subsequently settled there.
The Master was orphaned at a young age.
He served his mother with the utmost filial piety.
By nature he was quick-witted and possessed innate wisdom and insight.
He thoroughly investigated all ancient and modern classics, histories, and records without exception.
He was particularly profound in his mastery of Neo-Confucian philosophy (Lixue).
He cherished antiquity and excelled in poetic composition and versification.
Yet, his natural disposition was so simple and unassuming that it seemed as though he possessed no knowledge at all;
however, when engaging in discussion with guests,
he was like the Milky Way, whose shores and depths could not be discerned.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively among the lecture halls and mastered the teachings of Xianshou.
He once said:
"In study, what is valued is the penetration of the essential principle."
Words must necessarily accord with the meaning.
By using one's own intention to trace back to the original intent, one will grasp it;
the language and characters are merely dregs.
How could he have opened the eyes of wisdom for others?
Initially, while living in seclusion at Chengji, he built a dwelling and planted pines, intending to spend the rest of his days there;
thus, his contemporaries called him Master Songtang (Pine Hall).
Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty specially issued an edict appointing him as the abbot of Baima Monastery in Luoyang.
Scholars flocked to him like rivers rushing to the sea,
and his reputation spread far and wide day by day.
Emperor Chengzong established Wansheng Temple on Mount Wutai and issued an imperial decree seeking a founding first-generation abbot.
At that time, the Imperial Preceptor Kaluśri recommended him for the position.

King Seongjong immediately cast a golden seal and appointed him as State Preceptor of True Enlightenment (Jinguo Guoshi), overseeing the entire lineage of Buddhism and concurrently serving as the Abbot for the Protection of the State.
The Imperial Preceptor delivered the imperial decree to summon the Master.
The Master declined, saying:
"This mountain monk has already received the sovereign's bounty by residing at Baima Temple;
what virtue do I possess to dare preside over the protection of the state?"
To dwell beyond one's station brings misfortune;
to act without reflection is lack of clarity.
I am beset by these two afflictions.
"Please decline on my behalf," [the Emperor said].
The Imperial Preceptor replied,
"This is the supreme command of Your Majesty."
The Master’s devotion toward this temple was both diligent and sincere;
were it not for him, who else could have accomplished this?
This is a matter concerning the Buddhist teachings.
The Master skillfully carried this out.
Thus, having no choice but to proceed,
he traveled upon receiving his command and extensively propagated the Way of Qingliang.
Even unto old age, he never grew weary.
On the first day of the ninth month of the sixth year of the Dade era (the Renyin year), he manifested a slight illness;
he then preached the Dharma, took leave of the assembly, and passed away while sitting upright.
At the age of sixty-two, he was cremated;
his relics, numbering several hundred grains, were enshrined in a stupa at the foot of the Eastern Terrace.
His dharma successors included Hongjiao of Puning and Hantang of Pu'an.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yingbian of Jingfu Monastery in Qinzhou, Number Six The Śramaṇa Shi Yingbian of Bolin Tan in Qinzhou was titled Pujue.
His secular surname was Zhao.
When his hair still hung down in childhood locks, he became a *śrāmaṇera* for the purpose of driving away crows;
upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination.
At the age of twenty-five, he received the transmission of the teachings of Dharma Master Bolin Tan.
Before three years had passed, he emerged into the world at Jingfu Temple in Qinzhou.
His Way shook the great earth, and his fame spread across the four quarters.
He subdued heterodox views and raised the banner of the True Dharma.
By nature, his eloquence was as genuine and pure as uncut jade;
without the need for further carving or painting, people held him in deep esteem.
Even the fierce soldiers and martial men were able to revere him as the Buddha of a world without a Buddha.
Whenever they obtained offerings of cloth or money, he would use them all to establish Buddhist temples, provide for the Saṃgha, and give alms to the poor and destitute.
Upon hearing of his lofty character, Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty issued an edict to honor him for his exceptional virtue.
On the gengxu day of the sixth month in the first year of the Yanyou era, he passed away peacefully while seated amidst the assembly without prior illness;
on the evening of his death, as his bedding was being changed, extraordinary and radiant omens appeared.
The epitaph was inscribed on the remains following the cremation;
the stupa was erected behind Pujue Temple.
He had lived in this world for sixty-eight years.
He was sixty-one years old at the time of his death. 7.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Deqian of Chong’en Temple in the Capital. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Deqian of Chong’en Temple in the Capital, Number Seven. Shi Deqian’s style name was Fuyuan.
Her surname was Yang,
and she was a native of Dingping in Ningzhou.
From her youth, she served as a *karmadāna* and took delight in reciting Buddhist scriptures.
Upon reaching a slight maturity, he traveled through the regions of Qin, Luo, Bian, and Ru;
crossing north of the Yellow River, he visited the states of Qi, Wei, Yan, and Zhao to inquire after the teachings of the former virtuous masters.
Initially, he received the Prajñāpāramitā teachings from Master Ning in Binzhou.
He practiced the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* under Master Zhong of Yuanzhou;
he received profound assistance from Master Xian of Haoshi;
and he studied the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatāra-jñānālokālaṃkāra-sūtra* under Master Yi of Qianling.
He thoroughly studied treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Abhidharmakośa* under Master Ying at Shanzhou;
he listened to the commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* under Master Wen at Yangxia.
In total, these six sutras, four treatises, and one vinaya were all characterized by vast language and profound meaning, exhausting the depths of the Tripitaka.
These several masters were all renowned far and wide for their discernment of the Dharma and their understanding of its meaning.
Daoqian personally studied under them all, absorbing their teachings through close association, and he was determined to reach the ultimate path.
Later, he went to the capital to receive the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from the Grand Minister (Dà Sītú) and Abbot of the Wàn'ān Altar (Tánzhǔ).
Initially, by imperial decree, he resided at Wanningsi;
he was later transferred to Chongensi for ten successive periods.
His virtue and conduct were held in high esteem by the Emperor’s innermost thoughts.
His reputation spread beyond the seas, yet he never allowed his honor, fame, or imperial favor to alter his resolve.
He once said:
"The scholar clad in hempen robes stands aloof from the world."
If one has no cause for shame, even in hearing the Dharma in the morning and dying in the evening,
what more could one desire?
Having long resided in a great monastery, I have repeatedly been graced by imperial favor.
Valuing only the retirement from worldly affairs as the highest ideal,
he yielded his teacher’s seat to his disciples and withdrew to a secluded place,
declining all social engagements and confining himself within a single room like one who keeps his knowledge hidden in a bag.
He clarified his own brilliance and delighted in his own joy;
he dwelt in the world yet remained detached from it.
On the twenty-sixth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Yuanyan era, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
The Emperor bestowed fifty strings of cash as funeral subsidies.
He commanded the relevant authorities to prepare ceremonial guards,
banners, and musical ensembles to escort the remains to the cremation site.
He obtained several dozen śarīra relics and erected a stūpa at the southern corner of the city.
His worldly age was fifty-one,
and his monastic seniority was forty-three.
8. Biography of the Śramaṇa Śākya Dāyipa of Kyōto Keiujū-ji Temple The Śramaṇa Śākya Dāyipa of Kyōto Keiujū-ji Temple, number eight: Chos-skyid Śākya Dāyipa was of unknown nationality.
In his youth, he served as a bhikṣu to the Imperial Preceptor;
for thirteen years he attended upon him to listen to his discourses.
Having been molded and refined over such a long period, he was transformed into a vessel of great excellence.
All the Vinaya and Śāstra treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as those of the Secret Mantra section, have found their ultimate convergence in principle therein.
When the Imperial Preceptor was returning to the West,
[the Emperor] escorted him as far as Lintao and commanded that he rely upon the Great Being Chos kyi 'byung gnas (Choskyi Jungne).
In his nineteenth year, he heard what had never been heard before;
his realization of the Way became increasingly refined and concentrated.
The people of Qin requested that he reside at an ancient Buddhist temple.
He practiced all six *pāramitās* without exception and was simultaneously well-versed in the teachings of the Honored Head (Mañjuśrī). Consequently,
his reputation spread to the four quarters and his path was held in high esteem by the three courts.

When Emperor Wu of the Yuan dynasty ascended the throne, he summoned him to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma; his responses pleased the Emperor, who bestowed upon him generous gifts, which he declined and refused to accept.
Not long after, he requested leave to return home, and this was granted.
He resolved that he would devote himself to his final years there.
Shortly thereafter, he was summoned back to the capital.
He extensively propagated the Dharma teachings,
and the Emperor personally attended his sermons and specially conferred upon him the title of Tripitaka Master Hongfa Pujie (Great Propagation of the Dharma, Universal Salvation).
He was commanded to cast a golden seal and a purple square-cut robe to mark his extraordinary merit.
An imperial edict was issued requiring all princes, dukes, and high ministers to consult him on the essential points of the Dharma.
On the sixteenth day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Yan-you era, he passed away while sitting upright without illness.
He reached the age of seventy-three.
The Emperor ordered the two palaces to grant ceremonial silk to assist with the funeral.
The Crown Prince and the high ministers presented offerings, and the authorities were commanded to escort his remains and erect a stupa.

He was posthumously titled National Teacher Yousheng. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Miaowen of Baoji Temple in the Capital (9) The Great Virtuous Ming Shi Miaowen was the son of the Sun family of Weizhou. He was a śramaṇa at Baoji Temple in the capital. His character was refined and his learning vast; he was deeply versed in both the exoteric and esoteric teachings. During the Kaiyuan era, he traveled to Mount Wutai, where he encountered the Dharma Master Fazhen of the Huayan Temple. Fazhen had received the transmission of the *Mahāvairocana-sūtra* from the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha. Miaowen requested initiation into the ritual procedures and the secret mantras. Fazhen transmitted them to him, and Miaowen practiced them with great diligence. Later, when the Emperor summoned Fazhen to the capital, Miaowen followed him there. He subsequently served as the Abbot of the Eastern Pagoda of the Great Ci’en Monastery. He also presided over the ordination platforms at the Ximing and Chongfu monasteries, where he conferred the full precepts upon thousands of monks and nuns. He was also appointed as the Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices for the Imperial Ancestral Temple. In the second year of the Tianbao era, he was granted the purple robe and the title of National Teacher. In the third year of the same era, he was summoned to the palace to perform the rites of the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*. When the ritual was completed, the Emperor bestowed upon him the rank of Duke of the Second Order and the title of Great Master of the Golden Wheel. In the fifth month of the first year of the Changqing era, he fell ill and passed away at the age of seventy-one. He was buried at the foot of Mount Zhongnan. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of Great Master of the True Dharma. His disciples erected a stele at the temple to commemorate his virtues. His remains were interred at the site of his residence. His biography was recorded by the śramaṇa Shi Daoxian. The above is the ninth account. At the age of nine he left home to become a monk, and at eighteen he received full ordination.
Thereafter, he traveled to study in the regions of Yun, Shuo, Yan, and Zhao.
At twenty-one, he arrived at the capital.
Having studied the Perfect and Sudden Teachings under the Venerable Master Ming,
he remained submerged among the masses for eleven years. The assembly then requested him to emerge into the world and assume a monastic office.
At first, robed in red, he ascended the lion throne and unleashed his unimpeded eloquence like a mountain torrent rushing down a gorge;
yet when dwelling in seclusion, he was simple and silent, never uttering a word without due reflection.
His cultivation of the self was characterized by humility and restraint;
he had no desire for haste and never acted with impetuosity—his general conduct was largely of this nature.
At the age of forty-eight, he resided at Yunquan in Ji, where he practiced diligence and frugality.
The elders cherish its virtue,
while the juniors revere its teachings;
thus the community is harmonious and the monastery is well-ordered.
He used the surplus grain in the granaries to relieve the hungry people;
the inhabitants of Ji praised him.
Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and, turning to his attendants, said:
This was a monk of great merit; by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Baoji Monastery.

From that time forth, the Dharma assemblies flourished even more, with both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings proceeding side by side to provide universal salvation for both monastics and laypeople.
At that time, lecture halls throughout the land were in disarray, with scholars rigidly adhering to nominal characteristics (nāma-lakṣaṇa) and becoming mired in divergent paths.
Wén alone extensively propagated the Vaipulya sūtras and revitalized them through the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong).
He caused those who clung to the stump to attain integration within the realm beyond silence;
like dragons and elephants treading together, they vied to ride the Single Vehicle.
Having surpassed eighty years of age, he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi.
In the sixth year of the Yanyou era, knowing that the time had come, he instructed his disciples.
Raising his voice, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha;
facing west, he sat in the lotus posture and, forming the *samādhi-mudrā* with his hands, passed away in serene stillness.

The stupa was erected outside the Pingze Gate. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Liaoxing of Puning Temple on Mount Wutai (Part Ten): The śramaṇa Shi Liaoxing, whose secular name was [unrecorded], was styled Dalin. He was from Changzhou in Wu Commandery. His ancestors were of the Liu clan of the state of Qi. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, his great-great-grandfather, Liu Xian, served as the Governor of Changzhou. His grandfather, Liu Shou, served as the Administrator of Dongyang. His father, Liu Xuan, served as the Magistrate of Changshu. All three held office during the Liang dynasty. When the Chen dynasty rose, the family moved to the capital. His mother was the daughter of the General-in-Chief of the Left, Liu Zongzhi. She gave birth to him while residing at the Daming Palace. At the age of five, he entered the household of the Prince of Jingling, where he studied the *Laozi* and the *Zhuangzi*. At seven, he became a novice at the Zhongxing Temple in the capital. At twelve, he received full ordination under the Vinaya Master Huixiu of the Xingshan Temple. He was profoundly versed in the Vinaya and thoroughly understood the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra*. Later, he traveled to the capital to attend lectures on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. He also visited the various monasteries of the two mountains (Wutai and Tiantai) to seek out eminent masters. He eventually settled at Puning Temple on Mount Wutai. He lectured extensively on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra*. He also composed commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra*. He passed away on the twenty-third day of the second month in the third year of the Yongchang era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of sixty-four. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at the temple. He had one disciple named Daoyuan, who succeeded him in the lineage. Yuan later resided at the Jueyun Temple on Mount Wutai. He was a descendant of the House of Wu.
As a descendant of Duke Wu of Song, he took his posthumous title as his surname.
From his youth, he was fond of learning, possessing a natural intelligence and wisdom bestowed by Heaven.
Initially, he received the tonsure and the full precepts under Master An.
He attended various lecture halls to thoroughly investigate the Tripiṭaka.
Later, he encountered National Preceptor Jingue, who enlightened his mind.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively through Guanzhong, Shanxi, Hedong, Luoyang, Hanzhong, and Xiangyang,
seeking out men of venerable virtue from whom he studied.
These included the masters Bolin, Tantuan, Guanfu, Huainan, and Ci.
All were renowned in their time for their mastery of the Xianshou (Buddha-nature) teachings.
By nature, they all visited his gate to receive his profound instructions.
Upon returning, they further consulted Zhenjue at Longdi, whereupon [Zhenjue] said:
"The Buddhist Dharma's compass lies herein.
Subsequently, he traveled from Zhenjue to Mount Wutai;
before long, Zhenjue passed away.
He subsequently traveled north to Yan and Ji, concealing his traces beneath the gates of the Wei court.
He lived in leisure upon the rivers and seas, as if about to forget the world entirely.
Emperor Chengzong summoned him to reside at Wanningsi.
His reputation resounded both within and without.
During the Zhida era, the Empress Dowager founded a temple on Mount Wutai called Puning;
he was invited to reside there as its first patriarch.
As for the Master’s character, he was resolute and upright, possessing a strong sense of integrity.
He could not stoop to flatter or seek favor from others;
consequently, his footsteps never entered city walls or government offices, nor did he ever visit those in power or high station.
Some people were envious of him.
Xingwen once said:
"I was originally but a solitary bhikṣu, yet I have been favored by the Son of Heaven with the appointment to this great monastery."
I only pray that you will, day and night, propagate the Dharma without indolence;
occupied as you are with repaying the grace of the state,
what else could I possibly seek?
Although there were the slanderous words of Zang Cang against Gongli,
they were merely like blue flies settling on a jujube tree; yet,
seeing that my destiny was not met and the Way would not prevail, I put on my sandals and departed.
Where could he not go?
At that time, because Emperor Yuan Xuan favored the Western monks, their followers were extremely numerous;
when they went out or entered the palace, their mounted retinues were as grand as those of princes and dukes.
Some wore vermilion woolen caps and towering crowns, sitting with haughty self-importance;

yet among the renowned and virtuous masters of the world, there were none who did not pay them homage by drawing back their robes, touching their feet, and entreating them to stroke their heads and rub the crowns of their heads.
This is called "receiving [the disciple]";
the Master merely performed a long bow and then turned to address the assembly, saying:
"How could I dare to treat others with contempt?
I have heard that the gentleman loves others with ritual propriety (*li*).
How could I bend my will and bring humiliation upon myself?"
If one were to practice it through self-abasement,
it would be either sycophancy or flattery;
I act for the sake of the Way itself.
What was there to seek therein?
The wise held his meaning in high esteem.

Baoyan, whose courtesy name was Shiwei, was a native of Dalin. His family name was Shi. He was born in the year of the *jiachen* (68th year of the sexagenary cycle) during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. His father, Shi Xing, was a man of great virtue who lived in seclusion. When Baoyan was still a child, his father took him to visit the various monasteries to observe the monks' conduct. At that time, there was a monk named Huishou at the Guangzhai Temple in Chang'an; he was a man of profound learning and possessed great spiritual power. Upon seeing Baoyan, he remarked with admiration, "This child possesses the marks of a great vessel. He subsequently took him as a disciple and taught him the scriptures and treatises. Baoyan applied himself with diligence and mastered them thoroughly. Later, he traveled to the capital, where he resided at the Shengshou Temple. There, he encountered the Venerable Daoxuan, who was renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya.

Baoyan studied under him and became deeply versed in the precepts. He later returned to his home region and settled at Puan Temple on Mount Yushan. There, he devoted himself to meditation and recitation, and his reputation for piety spread far and wide. In the first year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, he passed away at the age of seventy-four. He was the younger son of the Kang family from Chengji;
having encountered the turmoil of war and loss, he shaved his head along with his younger brother to become a monk.
Later, he studied under Zhenjue, who transmitted the school of Xianshou and succeeded to its Way. He was a man of simple and sincere character, free from artifice;
the depths of his mind were as still as placid water.
When Zhijue attained true awakening and sat upon the site of enlightenment for the third time,
Yan and his younger brother both followed him to assist him.
After Zhijue entered nirvana, Yan succeeded him on the seat.
Without delay, he received an imperial decree to reside at both Pu’an and Youguo Monasteries, where he stayed for the longest period.
Together with Dalin Xingchao, he propagated the teachings of Qingliangshan extensively from both within and without.
On the seventh month of the second year of Zhizhi, he entered nirvana.
His worldly lifespan was fifty-one years.
A stupa was erected at the mouth of Fenggu Valley.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zhide of Tianxi Monastery in Jinling, Number Twelve. Shi Zhide, whose style name was Yunyan, heard the Dharma from Fazhao of Xixi. He was a śramaṇa of Tianxi Monastery in Jinling.
He was the son of the Liu family from Dongchang in Shandong.
At the age of twelve, he received the scriptures from Venerable Haiwen of Kaiyuan Temple in Shunde.
He heard that Dharma Master Fazhao of Xijing at Longxing Temple in Zhending was extensively propagating the fundamental tenets of the Ci'en school.
Jing followed him to study and fully mastered his profound teachings.
In the twenty-fifth year of the Zhizheng era (1358), an imperial edict was issued establishing thirty-six Imperial Lecture Halls throughout the various circuits of Jianghuai,
with the aim of seeking out those of authentic lineage and virtuous conduct to preside over them.
His virtue was such that he was selected by Emperor Sejo, who summoned him for an audience and granted him a banquet along with a purple square-cut robe.
He was appointed to preside over the two monasteries of Cheonheung and Jungjong.
For thirty-one years, he lectured daily on the commentaries of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
He was specially bestowed with the title "Master Foguang.
Whenever he conferred the precepts upon the seven assemblies of disciples,
he invariably instructed their parents and siblings to ensure they would not commit transgressions.
As for the practice of burning incense or setting fire to one’s head and fingers as a lifelong vow,
he engaged in these for a long time until he exhausted his robes and alms-bowl to renovate the halls, corridors, and pavilions of the temple.
Furthermore, during years of famine, he would cook congee to feed tens of thousands of starving people.
In the common customs of Jiankang, people prized fermented sweet wine and were fond of cultivating relationships with officials;
Daode alone restrained himself with the strictness of the law.
His followers were meticulous and refined in their conduct whether they were out or at rest.
If anyone misappropriates permanently endowed property, they shall be fined one hundred [units] for every unit of error;
thus, those who commit such offenses shall be expelled.
He resided at Tianxi for over thirty years.
He wore a single robe and a pair of sandals for the rest of his life, never changing them.
He would not eat after noon and sat in meditation through the night until dawn.
Through the hardships of his recitation, he lost his sight.
Suddenly, he dreamed that a Brahman monk invited him to occupy a high seat within the inner courtyard,
while flowers fell from the sky like rain. Thereupon,
he manifested a slight illness.
On the seventh day of the second month in the second year of the Zhizhi era, he continued reciting the sutras without ceasing.
Shortly thereafter, he took leave of the assembly, sat peacefully, and passed away.
His worldly age was eighty-eight.
The shrine remained for twenty-one days;
his countenance was ruddy and radiant as if he were alive.
Upon cremation, the śarīra relics were beyond counting.
The assembly numbered several tens of thousands.
The stupa was located at Zhangjiashan in Jiangning;
the scholar Zhao Mengfu composed the inscription for it.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Puxi of Puzhao Monastery in Zhenjiang, Number Thirteen The śramaṇa Shi Puxi of Puzhao Monastery in Zhenjiang, whose style name was Ji-xiang, was a person of no-thought (wu-nian). His courtesy name was Duan. Shi Puxi’s style name was Ji-xiang.
He was a native of Shandong.
He was tall in stature, with a dark and emaciated face that bore a resemblance to a Buddhist monk.
In his youth, he earnestly entreated his parents to allow him to leave the household life.
His parents reproached him, considering it a great failing that he had no offspring;
consequently, he married and raised two sons,
only after which he was finally able to become a śramaṇa.
He thoroughly investigated the Faxiang school of Ci'en and studied the treatises of the Yogācāra masters, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*).
In the twenty-fifth year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan dynasty, Emperor Shidebala established an imperial lecture hall in Jianghuai.
Puzhao was one of them. The Emperor issued an edict appointing the Master to preside over them.
Beyond his formal lectures, he recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra daily.
He made it his regular practice to recite ten fascicles daily.
He was personally well-acquainted with Wunian of Yun'nan,
who was a preeminent master of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
There was no one in the world who could surpass him.
Whenever he engaged in debate with his teacher regarding the principles of doctrine,
if there were even slight errors, the teacher would rectify them with authoritative words.
Duan also submitted with sincerity and praised him.
After his parinirvāṇa, his remains were cremated, and the relics were exceedingly abundant;
his disciples preserved these sacred bones.
It was stored in a lacquered casket and preserved for more than twenty years.
When the stupa was first constructed at Mount Yu in Dantu,
upon the moment it was placed inside the stupa, the casket was opened and inspected.
One sees only the śarīra relics adhering to the inner and outer wrappings like swarms of bees or clusters of ants;
when touched, they shimmer brilliantly.
Among the people of Zhenjiang, many have produced images [of them].
He established shrines for him in various locations and was honored as "Auspicious Buddha" (Śrī-buddha).

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zu’ěr of Jingxin Temple in Jiading, Suzhou. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zu’ěr of Jingxin Temple in Jiading, Suzhou: Shishi Ying, Zhuyù Jìng, and Shi Zu’ěr, whose courtesy name was Rìzhāng and alternative style name was Yòngzhuó. He was from Shishi [Stone Chamber]. His family name was Wáng, and his given name was Zǐshēng. He was a native of Jiading County, Suzhou. At the age of seven, he entered the household of Master Fǎzhào at Huáxiāng Monastery in Jiading. At thirteen, he received the tonsure under Master Fǎzhào. At eighteen, he received full ordination at the same monastery. He studied the Vinaya under Master Fǎzhào and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* under Master Fǎyuè. He also studied the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* under Master Fǎyuè. He further studied the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* under Master Fǎyuè. Later, he traveled to Mount Tiantai to study the teachings of the Tiantai school under Master Fǎyuè. He also visited various masters to inquire about the meaning of the scriptures. He subsequently returned to his home province and resided at Jingxin Temple. He lectured extensively on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. He also lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. He composed commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra*, and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. He also wrote commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. He produced over one hundred fascicles of writings. He passed away at the age of seventy-one. His remains were interred at the temple grounds. He had a disciple named Zhuyù Jìng, who succeeded him. He was the son of the Zhang family of Changshu, Suzhou.
After shaving his head, he traveled east to Siming.
At that time, Master Wugong was residing at Yanqing Temple.
Shishi Eikō resided at Yūō-ji,
where everyone treated him as an equal regardless of age. Later,

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yuanzhen of Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang. Regarding the biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yuanzhen of Xingsheng Temple in Songjiang, number three: the Śramaṇa Yuanzhen, whose style name was Yongzang...
He was a native of the Zhu family from Shanghai in Songjiang.
Having left home to become a monk, he received full ordination at Xingsheng Temple and inherited the teachings and contemplative practices of the Tiantai school.
His observance of the precepts was lofty and pure, and he had mastered a vast array of literary works.
He diligently practiced the ritual of repentance for the Lotus Sutra and the Amitābha Sutra.
When he had leisure, he transcribed various sutras of the Lotus Sutra;
according to circumstances, he expounded the Dharma and sat in meditation until dawn.
In the year of Yichou during the Hongwu era, he suffered a slight illness.
He requested a bath, wrote a verse, and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Forty-two years."
Without action and without cultivation,
there is birth and there is extinction;
it is like a single bubble upon the great ocean.
Truly returning to non-returning,
his mind wandered in empty purity;
sitting cross-legged, he passed away in profound stillness.

4. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Huirì of Shang Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou. The Śramaṇa Shi Huirì of Shang Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou, styled Dongming, was a native of Boziting. His secular surname was Li. He was born in the first year of the Yongxi era of the Tang dynasty (682). From childhood, he possessed a sharp intellect and a profound disposition. At the age of eight, he entered the monastery of his maternal uncle, where he received the tonsure and began his studies. By the time he reached fifteen, he had mastered the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and other treatises. Subsequently, he traveled to various regions to seek out teachers. He studied under the Venerable Daoxuan at the Great Ci'en Monastery in Chang'an, receiving full ordination from him. He also studied the Vinaya under the Venerable Huizhi at the Great Xingshan Monastery in the capital. Later, he visited the venerable masters Daoyue and Huiming at Mount Wutai, where he further refined his understanding of the monastic rules. In the second year of the Yonghui era (701), he returned to his home province. There, he encountered the Venerable Zhixian of the Great Xingshan Monastery in Yangzhou, who instructed him in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. He also studied the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* under the Venerable Zhiyan of the Great Xingshan Monastery in the capital. During the Kaiyuan era, he traveled to the Daxiangshan Monastery in the capital to study the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* under the Venerable Zhizhou. He also attended lectures on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* given by the Venerable Fazang at the Great Ci'en Monastery. In the third year of the Tianbao era (744), he traveled to the capital, where he resided at the Great Xingshan Monastery. He lectured extensively on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. In the fifth year, he returned to his home province and stayed at the Great Xingshan Monastery in Yangzhou. He lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. In the thirteenth year, he once more traveled to the capital and resided at the Great Xingshan Monastery, lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. In the sixteenth year, he returned to his home province and stayed at the Great Xingshan Monastery in Yangzhou, lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. In the nineteenth year, he again traveled to the capital and resided at the Great Xingshan Monastery, lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
