In the seventieth year, he returned to his home province and stayed at the Great Xingshan Monastery in Yangzhou, lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. In the seventy-third year, he once more traveled to the capital and resided at the Great Xingshan Monastery, lecturing on the *Mahāpraj
He was the son of the Jia family of Tiantai,
a great-grandson of Jia Sidao, the Chancellor of the Song dynasty;
at the time when Sidao was sentenced to penal exile, he was still a child.
Aspiring to seek renunciation, he relied upon Master Pingshan at Guangyan Temple in the county.
After several years, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
At the age of twenty-two, hearing that Master Baziting was lecturing on the Tiantai teachings at Chicheng, he hurried to the master’s seat.
Before long, he was able to grasp the great meaning.
His son, Ting, sighed and said:
"Casting a ball down a steep slope is not sufficient to illustrate the swiftness of his mental faculty."
"May my Way flourish greatly through you!
From that time on, the Master’s learning became deeply immersed and richly matured, and his reputation grew preeminent in his day.
One day, while dozing, he fell asleep.
Suddenly, he saw bamboo lying on the ground, and upon the bamboo was white gruel, glistening and bright.
The Master lay on the ground and ate it.
Upon waking, he spoke of this to Zuting.
Ting provided an explanation, saying:
"The word for 'bamboo' (zhú) has the same pronunciation as 'congee' (zhōu).
You may thus eat it on the spot."
"Is it perhaps not because the conditions for my presence lie in Upper and Lower Tianzhu?
Thereupon, he crossed the Qiantang River to pay his respects to Master Jing of Zhuyu at Upper Tianzhu.
The quarters where he stayed were quite low and damp.
He then composed a poem to stir his feelings.
When Zhuyu saw the poem, he said to the assembly,
"This youth is no ordinary man."
"In the future, you shall become the master of this mountain;
it cannot be entrusted to one of such young years.
Therefore, I have met you as if you were a guest or a friend."
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed by imperial decree to the Office of the Guest Receptionist to oversee the monastic registers.
When Zhuyue passed away, Master Tanzang Cheng succeeded him on the seat;
Master Qi was then invited to reside in the rear hall.
After more than a year, he went forth to serve as the abbot of Rushan Shengshui.
In the fourth year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he resided at Jianfu Temple.
He served for three years before descending to Tianzhu, where the temple suffered a disaster.
The former minister Gao Nalin requested that the Master renovate it.
When the temple buildings were completed, Wang Meng composed a record for them.
In the fourth year, he moved to Upper Zhushan.
The Master knew that his karmic conditions were rooted in former lives and was never indolent day or night.
He personally oversaw the construction of every structure within the monastery.
When Emperor Shun of the Yuan dynasty heard of this, he specially bestowed upon him the title "Compassionate Light, Wondrous Response, Universal Salvation."
He was summoned back by means of a golden-embroidered robe.
In the sixteenth year, he withdrew into seclusion among the crags of Kuaiji,
where no one recognized him.
The former Chancellor Dashi Temür dispatched an envoy who, having identified him,
earnestly petitioned for his return to the mountains.
He resided at Upper Zhù for a total of twenty-five years.
In the second year of the Hongwu era of our Great Ming Taizu, he was summoned by imperial decree to the Buddhist assembly at Mount Jangshan.
The Ministry of Rites was ordered to provide him with meals.
On the following day, he was called upon for an audience in the Fengtian Hall.

The hundred officials assembled like a string of fish, yet the Master alone, being of the highest seniority, with his ruddy countenance and white eyebrows, took his place at the head of the ranks. The Emperor personally questioned him regarding the Way of delivering those submerged in darkness to salvation.
The Master presented his report, which met with the Emperor’s approval.
Emperor Taizu turned to the assembly of monks and said, "Lately, those who study Buddhism have done nothing but eat their fill and live in leisure, letting the years slip away in obscurity.
Texts such as the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Heart Sūtra* are all essential for the concentration of the mind."
"Why not investigate and exhaustively study its meaning?
If there are points you do not understand, you should consult Master Baimei.
Thereafter, whenever Emperor Taizu summoned him for an audience, he addressed him only as "Baimei" and did not call him by his name.

Once, while I was partaking of a meal in the imperial palace with Master Biefeng, Dharma Master Jinbifeng, and others, I petitioned that Waguan Temple—the site where the Sui dynasty’s Great Master Zhizhe expounded the Lotus Sūtra—must not be abolished. Consequently, the Taizu Emperor ordered the construction of separate quarters at Tianjie Monastery to preserve its traces.
By imperial decree, he was immediately appointed to open the mountain and preach the Dharma.
In the first month of spring in the fifth year, he again established a Great Water-Land Assembly at Mount Zhong, where the Master was commanded to expound the Vinaya precepts;
Emperor Taizu personally led the hundred officials to attend and listen.
When his affairs were concluded, he took leave to return to Upper Zhushan.
He resigned from his monastic duties and daily practiced the Amitābha Repentance to perfect his pure karma.
In the seventh month of the autumn of the twelfth year, one night he had a dream.
A blue lotus flower grew from within a square pond, its fragrance pervading the air.
Upon awakening, he told the assembly,
"I have seen an auspicious omen of my birth in the Pure Land."
In the world of men, he was indeed not far [from the ultimate goal].
Four days later, he sat in the lotus posture with palms joined and passed away.
His worldly age was eighty-nine.
His monastic seniority was seventy-three years.
Ten days later, his entire body was enshrined in the Miaoying Pagoda Cloister on the western peak of the temple.
From birth, his physical stature had been tall and imposing.
His eyebrows were more than an inch long,
and his eyes flashed with a piercing light that struck those who saw him.
Regardless of their age, whether old or young, all people perceived the Master as he entered the city.
Everyone cried out,
"The White-Browed Bhikṣu has come!
and they vied with one another to hold aloft incense and flowers, scattering them over him.
The Master’s countenance was stern and cold, and he did not utter a word frivolously.
Even when facing kings, dukes, and high ministers, he never produced a single word of flattery;
yet, when it came to guiding and attracting his junior disciples, his speech and expression were as warm as the light of spring.
Consequently, many people joyfully followed his teachings.
Those who succeeded him in the Dharma included several individuals, such as Siji, Xingshu, Yunjian, Yunzhong, Liangjin, Puzhi, Wenhui, Yuangxiu, and Jingfan.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Tu-zhang of Jiqing Temple in Hangzhou The Śramaṇa Shi Tu-zhang of Jiqing Temple in Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Yuanpu, was a man of the Five Heavens whose mind was as clear as crystal and who excelled in the transmission of the Dharma. His secular surname was Shi.
He was the son of Wang of Haining in the commandery.
From birth, a protruding brow-vein (fu-xi) ran across his forehead;
his eyes were bright and black as if painted with lacquer.
From childhood, he would not consume pungent or rich foods;
whenever his parents would secretly test him with such, he would immediately vomit uncontrollably.
He took delight in reading Buddhist scriptures.
A monk from a neighboring temple requested his father, saying,
"This child is of the Śākya clan."
"Why do you not beg for troops from me?
His father said in anger,
"My son is like a *puṇḍarīka* flower."
He was not like his peers;
he subsequently left home and entered Chuánfǎ Temple to receive the five precepts.
At that time, Liù Guàn, a Palace Secretary and Attendant-in-Ordinary, once stayed at the temple quarters.
His teacher then bestowed upon him the Classics and Histories,
personally expounding their profound meanings for him.
Upon hearing them, the Master understood them as if cutting through wood with a blade.
At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and became a full monk.
When Master Wufa of my monastery presided over Tianzhu,
the Master [Wufeng] took up his staff and traveled there to attend upon him.
Suddenly, he dreamed that he was traveling to a treasure realm.
There, a great Bodhisattva instructed him to kneel with his right knee on the ground and pay homage, orally reciting a text for repentance.
Upon waking, he reflected upon it and realized it was the verse text from the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" of Samantabhadra.
When he finally saw me at my hermitage, he gazed at me with wide-eyed attention.
He received from me, in due order, all the scriptural commentaries and doctrinal principles of the Tiantai school of teaching and contemplation.
With single-minded devotion and diligent study without slackening, he reached the point of forgetting both sleep and food.
I, Yin, personally observed his diligence and always expected him to achieve something vast and far-reaching.
At that time, Tianxin was pure and refined in heart; he was lofty and would not serve others, which is why the world called him "Yitiger" (the Tiger of Meaning).
He also admired Master Yi’s conduct and agreed to engage in debate by lamplight;
day after day they refuted and challenged one another with such precision that they reached the finest hairs.
The assembly declared them to be "two jewels."
After some time, Woe-ām passed away.
Master Il-po of Dongmyeong succeeded him on the seat, molding and refining his disciples.
He selected Master Seon to serve as the head of the monastic department.
He was appointed as the guest master and subsequently took charge of the affairs of the *sāṃghāṭī* (confession).
In the thirteenth year of the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, he received the imperial mandate to serve as the abbot of Qizhen Monastery.
This monastery was situated adjacent to the two monasteries of Nanzhu and Yanfu.
At that time, there were two masters of immense talent who excelled their predecessors and succeeded them; they resided there.
The Master, feeling his own learning was still insufficient, went daily to consult them.
He analyzed every subtlety of the profound teachings and contemplations, as well as the nuances of the partial and the perfect, the provisional and the real, one by one, leaving nothing unclarified.
Therefore, I have often sighed before the assembly, saying:
"The treasury of the Buddha's teachings is as vast as the ocean;
it is certainly not something that can be fully exhausted by one who seeks only personal excellence."
If I were to paint my own portrait and fail to advance,
how could I avoid the reproach of being narrow-minded and ignorant?
In the twentieth year, I moved to serve as abbot at Jingde Temple.
At the end of the Yuan dynasty, the world was in great turmoil due to the chaos of war.
While everyone else was preoccupied with securing their own safety,
the Master alone devoted himself single-mindedly to the affairs of the monastery.
He did not allow worldly hardships to alter his resolve.
His reputation for praising the good and censuring the evil caused people’s perceptions to change;
he daily received pure monastics and lectured on the commentaries of the sutras.
At that time, not a single moment was spent in vain.
When my Imperial Majesty’s brilliant Hongwu era reached the year of Jiqing and the seat remained vacant,
Prefect Li invited me to preside over the teaching of the Buddhist scriptures.

Before long, the Zhongshu (Secretariat) received an imperial decree ordering that the abbots of the famous monasteries of the five prefectures east and west of Zhejiang were to assemble in the capital to jointly pave the grounds of Tianjie Monastery and establish the Shanshi Yuan (Institute for the Propagation of the Good).
He was appointed to oversee the monastic community and supervise the construction work.
While the venerable elders from all quarters were at a loss as to what to do,
the Master alone devised a strategic plan, complete with systematic organization.
At that time, the assembly of one hundred thousand people all followed his example.
On the sixteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he foreknew that the time had come;
he summoned his disciples and entrusted them with his final instructions.
On the seventeenth day, he sat peacefully and passed away;
his age was forty-six,
and his years since ordination were twenty-eight.
After his cremation, his disciples Yuanjue, Yinyin, Shengyuan, Keqin,
and others enshrined his remains in a casket and erected a stupa south of the Stupa of Dharma Master Biancai at Longjing.
The Master’s character was refined and elegant; his discourses were passionate and forthright as he adhered to the direct path rather than conforming to worldly customs.
Whenever he sought to establish monasteries, those who would have fostered factions and cliques viewed him as a source of resentment.
The Master then vowed never to shave his head or take on disciples.
Whenever a student came to pay their respects with the desire to become his follower,
he would invariably reject them with firm words.
Not a single person was recorded falsely.
6. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Ruqi of Yanfu Temple in Hangzhou. The Śramaṇa Shi Ruqi, whose courtesy name was Ju’an and alternative style name was Taipo, [is here recorded].
He received the Dharma from Master Mingwen Haihui, who succeeded to the lineage of the late patriarchs.
The Master’s learning surpassed that of his peers and his talent excelled those of the Three Teachings;
it was not merely a mastery of the Ten Vehicles, the Three Contemplations, the Nine Classics, or the Seven Histories.
He was extensively versed in all the worldly names, terminology, and secret scriptures.
His Majesty, the Great Emperor Taizu, issued an imperial decree commanding him to reside at Tien-chieh (Heavenly Realm),
where he daily expounded the Buddhist teachings with various venerable elders to prepare for imperial inquiries.

By imperial decree, Zongle was commissioned to edit and annotate the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*, which were subsequently promulgated throughout the empire.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Datong of Baolin Monastery, Shaoxing. (Seven) Chungu Valley.
Gu Huizhao succeeded Jiang En;
Huiji and Tian'an followed Jie.
Gulimao Shi Datong, whose courtesy name was Yiyun,
took Biefeng as his pen-name.
He was the son of Wang of Shangyu in Yue.
The father’s friend, Chen Shi, the mother of the Master,
was ten months pregnant when her husband was sitting in the hall during the day;
suddenly, he saw an extraordinary monk with a bushy beard enter, shaking his mendicant’s staff.
The father rose and bowed, saying,
"From where have you come, Master?
He replied, "From Mount Kunlun."
Having finally pushed open the door and rushed inside in hot pursuit,
he heard the sound of a child crying in the room.
The father laughed and said:
"Could it be that my son is one who has returned from a previous life?
As a youth, the Master was brilliant and quick-witted; whenever he read a book, he immediately grasped its profound mysteries.
Initially, he practiced the composition of prose and verse with such elegance that his work was truly remarkable."
Thereupon, his father entrusted him with the continuation of the family’s scholarly tradition.
His mother alone sighed and said,
"This son possesses the seed of *prajñā*."
How could he be allowed to remain mired in the toil of worldly defilements?
He was accordingly ordered to enter Chongsheng Temple in Kuaiji to shave his head.
It was heard that Dharma Master Chungung was lecturing on the essential tenets of the Qingliang school at Jingde Temple in the commandery.
He went to rely upon him and fully received his transmission.
He further visited Master Gaohuai Zhao to refine his practice of the Contemplation of the Four Dharma Realms.
Subsequently, he moved from Chonggu to become the abbot of Baolin.
He then said to the Master,
"Your learning is both refined and extensive;
yet I fear your mind may become stalled in coarse attachments."
Merely increasing one's learning only binds one to intellectual views;
it is truly not the foundation for seeing into one's nature.
You should cultivate in seclusion and cleanse yourself of these attachments.
May this be a blessing for our lineage.
Thereupon, he was commanded to go to Qiantang to see the Chan Master Huiji Xi.
As soon as he saw the Master waving his fly-whisk, the Master’s long-standing habits of learning and hearing were instantly swept away.
He alone preserved his solitary brilliance, illuminating himself with a steady light.
Thus he passed six seasons of cold and heat.
Hei Ji deeply admired his resolve.
Furthermore, hearing of the flourishing Dharma path of Tianmu Zhongfeng, he went there to study under him,
intending to spend the remainder of his life there.
One day, Zhongfeng summoned him and exhorted him, saying:
The school of the Venerable Master [Xuanzang] has become increasingly distant and diminished with each passing day.
Your capacity is sufficient to restore it;
do not let yourself linger here for long.
He specially composed a verse of praise for the Qingliang image and sent it with the messenger.
The Master was greatly delighted and said,
"Only now do I understand that the myriad dharmas are fundamentally rooted in the one mind."
He did not know which was Chan and which was Teaching.
He returned to Baolin Monastery and again attended upon Chonggu, reporting the intent of Zhongfeng.
Chonggu immediately ordered him to share the seat and lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
At that time, Xu Tianyou and Wang Yijian, former officials of the Song dynasty, together extolled his reputation until his fame shone brightly.
Lord Fan, the Prefectural Governor, took pity on the venerable age of Changu Valley.
When the Venerable Yufeng yielded his seat,
he prepared the *īśvara-pūpa* offerings and spoke personally with the Master.
The Master’s countenance shifted with solemn gravity as he said:
What is most esteemed in the Way lies in the distinction between teacher and disciple.
This clarity can serve as an instruction for future students;
were one to take advantage of his old age to usurp his position, it would be a grave error.
"How could this be something done by a human being?
Your Excellency truly loves me,
yet you cause me to fall into a trap of reputation and principle."
This was truly a cause for injury.
Fan, unaware, rose from his seat and apologized, saying,
"My teacher is indeed no ordinary man."
"How could this be something I am capable of knowing?
In the early years of the Yuan Yanyou era, he went forth to preside over Jingtu Temple in Xiaoshan,
and subsequently moved to Jingde Temple.
In the Zhizhen era, he was commanded to reside at Dongta in Jiahe,
which was subsequently renamed Baolin.
However, Baolin was originally the site where National Teacher Qingliang pursued his studies.
Everyone honored the Master.
Yet the Master remained reclining in high repose and did not go.
Thereupon, the local commanderies and districts submitted joint petitions to invite him, and he came once more.
He first rolled up his sleeves and rose;
then, following the precedent of the thatched hall at Zhongnan,
he cleared a secluded dwelling to attract and welcome men of talent and virtue.
Consequently, among the scholars of the world, there were none who did not carry their bamboo cases upon their shoulders and tread upon their straw sandals to gather beneath his wheel.
At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he was bestowed the title "Buddha-Mind, Compassionate Aid, Wondrous Eloquence" (Fóxīn Cíjì Miàobiàn) along with a golden-embroidered *saṃghāṭī* robe.
The former minister Zhongjie Taibuhua was governing Yue when a severe drought occurred.
He earnestly entreated the Master to offer prayers on his behalf.
The Master burned incense from his own arm at the Xuandu Pagoda, whereupon it rained heavily and profusely.
At the end of the Yuan dynasty, the empire was in great chaos and the temple was destroyed by fire.
The Master resolutely planned to rebuild it anew.
When our Great Emperor Taizu ascended the throne, he established a *wu-cha* (unrestricted) great assembly at the Bell [Pagoda].
Mount [Wu] summoned the Master to an audience in the Wulou Hall.
At that time, the Master was eighty years old and was exempted from prostrating and kneeling.
The following day, he was granted a banquet within the imperial palace.
Upon the conclusion of the ceremony, he was presented with several ingots of white gold from the inner treasury along with rare treasures to honor his departure.
The master’s spiritual countenance was transcendent; the *vṛṣa* mark on his forehead was prominent, and a *śikhā* (cranial protuberance) extended through the crown of his head.
His stature was tall and majestic, his bearing upright, and his speech elegant;
he appeared like a prince or nobleman. Whenever there were those who sought to challenge the teaching, the Wheel of Dharma rolled on.
If the principle were not upright,
even with the axe and block before him, he would not allow his spirit to be diminished in the slightest;
even if they were to apply dangerous laws against him, he would not look back at them even a little.
He made it his constant practice to recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
and within a few days, the man died of his own accord.
The Master always supported other schools of thought without the slightest hint of suspicion or prejudice.
For instance, when Danjiang was a student at Shaolin, he recommended him to serve as the abbot of Tianti;
and when Tian'an was a follower of the Tiantai teachings,
he entreated him to reside at Yuan Tong.
The Master traveled to Min.
At that time, Gulin Mao was the abbot of Baoning in Fujian,
and his discipline of subordinates was excessively strict.
A certain unscrupulous monk from Chu was about to lodge a complaint with the government office.
The Master happened to encounter him at a guesthouse and,
having prepared a sumptuous meal, served it to him with composure, saying:
I was originally unfamiliar with Gulin.
I have heard that it is a renowned and virtuous Zen monastery;
you people will likely seek to bring harm to it.
"How can a gentleman regard such as you as worthy people?
It would be better to desist;
otherwise, I fear you will bring great calamity upon yourselves."
The matter was subsequently dropped.
By nature, the Master was profoundly filial and regretted having lost his father so early;
whenever he reached the anniversary of his father’s death, he would invariably weep incessantly.
Her fostering mother’s devotion was pure and ultimate;
it did not merely consist of complying with her wishes or providing physical comfort,
but necessarily ensured that her mind partook of the flavor of the Way.
Furthermore, he ensured that the ancestral sacrifices were never omitted.
He also requested a renowned Confucian scholar to compose a biography so that a stone monument might be erected beside his tomb.
The Master observed the Vinaya with extreme rigor; apart from a single alms bowl, he possessed no superfluous belongings.
He possessed only some five thousand scrolls of books and historical records.
In the twelfth month of the second year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness.
On the tenth day of the final spring month of the following year, he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma.
He took leave of the assembly and returned to his quarters; sitting upright, he passed away.
His secular age was eighty-two, and his years as a monk were sixty-five.
There were many extraordinary signs during his cremation.
A stupa was erected on Zhushan Mountain.
Among his writings are the *Tianzhu Gao* (Drafts from Mount Tianzhu) and the *Baolin Leibian* (Categorized Compilation of Baolin), each consisting of several volumes.

The Dharma heirs who succeeded him include: Daoyan of Miaoxin, Shanxian of Gaotingshan, Ruolan of Goryeo, Renjing of Jingdesi, Mingshan of Jiangshan, Shiyi of Yanshousi, Guochen of Nanta, Dahui of Fucheng, Xingcheng of Jingfusi, Dao’ni of Miaoxiangsi, Daoyue of Fayunsi, Fan’ao of Jingtusi, Riyi of Baolinsi, and others.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Shaoyong of Anguo Temple in Shanghai, Songjiang. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Shaoyong of Anguo Temple in Shanghai, Songjiang, Number Eight. The śramaṇa Shi Shaoyong of Jing’an Temple was styled Suichu.
He was the son of the Chen family of Shanghai.
At the age of thirteen, his parents entrusted him to Ankuo Temple in his village.
There, he received the Dharma from the Dharma Master Jing’an Zhen.
By nature gifted with keen intelligence and maintaining strict observance of the precepts,
he first went forth to preach the Dharma at Changqing Temple in Hangzhou.
He fully unfolded the profound winds of the Way, and both monastics and laypeople turned toward his transformative influence.
He subsequently moved to Cigan Temple in Wuxing.
At that time, Dharma Master Shouren of Changgan in Jinling invited him to occupy the first seat,
and the entire assembly bowed in reverence.
In the Guiyou year of the Hongwu era, he was summoned to attend to affairs at Mount Lu.
His responses during the imperial audience pleased the Emperor, who bestowed upon him a gold-threaded *saṃghāṭī* robe and promoted him to the rank of Right Lecturer on the Sutras.
Before long, he was promoted to the position of Right Supervisor of the World (You Shanshi).

On the fifth day of the first month of the Chou year, he manifested slight illness and passed away while sitting upright. Upon hearing the news, His Majesty issued an imperial decree dispatching a palace attendant to present sacrificial offerings.
On the day of the cremation, several thousand people accompanied the funeral procession. His disciples collected his *śarīra* relics and enshrined them in a stupa at An Guo Temple.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Jujing of Puzhao Temple in Songjiang (9) The biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Jujing of Puzhao Temple in Songjiang, number nine: Dongyuan Shi Jujing, whose courtesy name was Xinyuan and whose alternative style was Lansue.
His learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular texts; he was skilled in composition and refined in the Vinaya.
He served as the guest prefect under Master Yiyu at Dabao’en Temple in Jinling.
Later, he studied under Master Dongyuan of Jiqing Temple in Hangzhou.
He occupied the first seat in the Chanmota Hall and subsequently lectured on the *I Ching*.
At the beginning of the Yongle era,
he was summoned [to court].
By imperial decree, he was commissioned to collate the Tripitaka and participate in the compilation of the Imperial Compendium of Rites (*Huidian*).
Subsequently, he resided as abbot at Guangfu Jangsi Monastery in Shanghai,
and later moved to Puzhao Monastery in Songjiang, where he presided over the Dharma assembly for thirteen years.
He constructed the Daxiong Hall, the Haoyue Hall, and the Three Gates of Liberation;
the corridors, multi-tiered eaves, and the Xiangji Hermitage were resplendently renovated.
The seven assemblies gazed upon him with reverence, and the influence of his Way spread far and wide.

10. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Puzhi of Longjing Monastery in Hangzhou. The śramaṇa Shi Puzhi of Longjing Monastery in Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Wuyi and pen-name was Yizhi Sǒu, [is here recorded].
A native of the Zhao family from Linping, Zhejiang,
he left the household life at Longjing Temple in Qiantang. There,
he relied upon the Dharma Master Dongming Ri to receive instruction in the Tiantai doctrine of the inherent nature (xingju).
He excelled in lecturing and exposition.
Having visited the four great monasteries, his teaching style was widely acclaimed.
In his later years, he opened a seat for instruction at Yanqing Temple in Songjiang.
He thus devoted himself to the exclusive cultivation of Pure Land practices until the end of his life, never ceasing regardless of cold or heat.
On the second day of the first month in the Wuzi year of the Yongle era, he fell slightly ill;
he gathered the assembly, sat upright facing west, and passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.

He once compiled the *Commentary on the Shorter Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* in one fascicle. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Shanqi of Yanqing Monastery in Suzhou (Fascicle 11). The Śramaṇa Shi Shanqi of Yanqing Monastery in Suzhou: His courtesy name was Dongbai, and his alternative style name was Xiaohan. He was a native of Changzhou in Wujun Prefecture. From childhood, he possessed a sharp intellect and was naturally inclined toward the Way. At the age of twelve, he left home to become a novice under the guidance of the Venerable Master Daoyuan of Xiangguo Monastery in Wujun. Subsequently, he traveled to various regions to seek instruction from eminent masters. He studied the Vinaya under the Venerable Master Zhiyi of Huqiu Monastery in Suzhou, and the Mahāyāna teachings under the Venerable Master Zhixu of Yunqi Monastery in Yangzhou. He also received the full precepts from the Venerable Master Shouzhong of Jingshan Monastery in Yangzhou. Later, he resided at Yanqing Monastery in Suzhou, where he devoted himself to the practice of meditation and the cultivation of wisdom. He frequently lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*. He also composed commentaries on the *Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*. He passed away in the spring of the second year of the Yongzheng era (1724) at the age of sixty-four. His remains were interred at the monastery. His writings include the *Lectures on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the *Lectures on the Lotus Sūtra*, the *Lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Commentary on the Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*, the *Record of the Dharma Garden*, the *Collection of Dharma Talks*, and the *Anthology of Zen Sayings*, totaling over twenty fascicles. His dharma heirs included the Venerable Master Xingzhen of Lingyan Monastery in Suzhou, the Venerable Master Xingyin of Xuefeng Monastery in Fuzhou, the Venerable Master Xingxian of Xuefeng Monastery He was the son of the Yang family of Changzhou in Gusu.
His lineage had been an official clan for generations.
As soon as he was able to speak, he was already proficient in the Buddhist scriptures as if he had been familiar with them from birth.
His parents regarded him with wonder;
recognizing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, they sent him to enter Yongmao Monastery to become a monk.
Before long, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He lived in seclusion at Longshan, where he exhaustively researched the Great Canon;
there was no history among the hundred schools that he did not master thoroughly.
In the fifth year of the Yongle era (1408), he emerged from retreat to serve as abbot at Yanqing Temple in his native district.
The following year, he was summoned to compile the *Yongle Dadian* and to collate the Tripitaka.
He was granted a gold-embroidered *saṃghāṭī*.
At that time, renowned figures such as Shen Minwang, Wang Ruyu, and Qian Yuanpu all became his "external friends" (fangwai jiao).
Someone argued for the differences between Confucianism and Buddhism.
The Master said:
"Setting aside the fact that the principles of the sages are the same, each merely established its own teaching."
It is further said:
"In both the transmission of the Way by the East (China) and the realization of nature by the West (India), none prioritize anything more than honoring the fundamental roots.
Therefore, although we have departed from our parents, in matters of nourishing life and sending off the dead, we invariably follow the principle of abundance."
He was extremely affectionate toward his brothers.
He passed away in the Guihai year of the Zhengtong era;
his stupa was enshrined at Longshan.

12. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yingneng of Shoufu Monastery in Hengzhou, Guangxi. Regarding the biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yingneng of Shoufu Monastery in Hengzhou, Guangxi, number twelve: Shi Yingneng’s assumed surname was Yang.
He was indeed Prince Jianwen. The eldest son of Crown Prince Yiwen and the legitimate grandson of the Taizu, he was invested as the Imperial Grandson (Huangsunsun).
His name was Yunwen.
At birth, his cranial dome was somewhat tilted; the Taizu stroked him and said, "A half-moon child."
Furthermore, he was exceptionally brilliant in his studies.
One night, when Crown Prince Yiwen and his attendants were reciting a poem on the new moon as ordered by Taizu, the Prince composed this verse:
"Yesterday at Yanling, the fishing hook was lost."
Who can move it to the crest of the azure clouds?
Though its perfect, round form has not yet been attained,
its pure radiance already pervades the nine continents.
The Crown Prince recited:
"Who has taken these jade-like fingernails / To carve marks upon the heavens?"
"The shadow falls into the rivers and lakes;

dragons and serpents dare not swallow it. When Taizu read this, he was displeased, for the phrase "the shadow falls into the rivers and lakes" was not an auspicious omen, as it implied that he had not yet achieved complete unification.
In the thirty-first year of the Hongwu era, when the Great Ancestor was nearing his end,
he entrusted him with a small casket,
its seal and lock being extremely secure.
The observance of the precepts was relaxed only during times of urgent difficulty.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month of this year,
he ascended the throne at the age of twenty-three.
The following year, the reign title was changed to Jianwen.
Fang Xiaoru was summoned to serve as a Court Attendant (Hanlin Shijiang) and entered the Wen yuan Pavilion,
where he lectured daily on the *Rites of the Zhou*.
He altered the old regulations established by Taizu;
consequently, many of the princes became insolent and disrespectful,
so he responded by showing them excessive courtesy and bestowing special favors upon them.

Huang Zicheng, Grand Master for Attendant Reading and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and Qi Tai, Minister of War, deliberated on the plot to curtail the power of the princes, prioritizing the Prince of Yan.
They ordered Vice Minister Zhang Bing and Commander-in-Chief Xie Gui to monitor the Prince of Yan’s movements.
He subsequently pressured Yan to rise in arms for the "Pacification of the Rebellion" (*Jingnan*).
He campaigned southward against Huang and Qi.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of Jianwen, he breached the Jinchuan Gate; the Emperor set fire to the palace and burned it down.
He opened the late Emperor Taizu’s remaining casket and examined its contents.
Inside he found Yang Yingneng’s ordination certificate, a razor, a *kāṣāya*, and black robes.
He thereupon shaved his hair and departed from the Imperial Canal to wander the four quarters as a monk.
From Huxiang he entered Shu;
from Yunnan he returned to Min and entered Guangxi, where he resided at Nanshan Shoufo Temple in Hengzhou for fifteen years.
Whenever he ascended the seat to expound the Dharma, those who returned were exceedingly numerous;
wherever he went, he established great assemblies of the Dharma,
such that people did not realize he was the Emperor.
He then traveled to Nanjing and resided at a Xiao temple.
Disciples gathered there like clouds, and the Master provided them with teachings according to their needs;
the entire assembly was filled with joy.
After a long time, he arrived at Sien Prefecture.
Standing in the middle of the road, he encountered the Prefect as he was coming out;
his attendants shouted at him.
The Master said,
"I am Emperor Jianwen.
I have traveled from Yunnan through Fujian and arrived here."
Now that I am old,
I wish to escort my remains back to the imperial capital.
Upon hearing this, the Imperial Intendant reported it to the court, who bestowed upon me the title "Old Buddha."
He ordered a postal relay to escort him to the capital,
whereupon he composed a poem, saying:
"Wandering through rivers and lakes for forty autumns."
Returning home, I find snow filling my hair;
the universe holds its grief, where is my home?
The Yangtze and Han rivers are heartless, their waters flowing on of their own accord.
Cloud-shadows darken within the Changle Palace;
the sound of rain brings sorrow to the Zhaoyang Hall.
The new rushes and slender willows turn green year after year.
The village elders wept in stifled sobs without ceasing.
Upon reaching the capital, the court had not yet ascertained whether the report was true or false;
however, because the eunuch Wu Liang had previously attended the Emperor’s meals, [he was summoned].
He sent someone to investigate him.
When the master saw Liang, he immediately called out,
"Are you not Wu Liang?"
He replied, "No.
The Master said,
"In the past, when I was presiding in the private audience hall, I..."
Once, I discarded a piece of meat on the ground;
you prostrated yourself and licked it up to eat.
How could you have forgotten this?
Liang prostrated himself and wailed with great grief.
Thereafter, he took [the remains] into the Western Palace to offer them worship, and they ultimately passed away within the palace. The Epilogue says:
Once Emperor Jianwen succeeded to the great mandate as the second sovereign,
his worthy ministers vigilantly adhered to the established laws of the Grand Ancestor, supplementing those points that had not yet been fully realized.
Then Emperor Wen would have remained content in his princely residence;
how could there have been the "Pacification of the Rebellion" army breaking through the Jinchuan Gate?
It was because he once mistakenly employed those such as Fang Xuanling and Huang Fu.
He lectured on the *Rites of Zhou* and the implementation of the well-field system.
How could Emperor Wen have sat idly by while the Great Treasure was being destroyed by a dwarf,
folding his hands and waiting to be bound?

The fact that the state has enjoyed such prosperity and the world has been so peaceful for several hundred years now truly depends upon that single expedition during the "Suppression of the Rebellion.
In the *Ganshan ji* (Ganshan Collection), the matter of Jianwen is discussed in depth, stating that once one has suffered such a calamity, there is absolutely no reason to leave the secular life.
Once one has left the household life, there is absolutely no possibility of returning to the palace.
Yang Yingneng’s memorial was a fabrication based on these facts.
This account is recorded here according to the historical precedents of our dynasty found in the *Huangming tongzai*, the *Xianzhang lu*, and the *Sishen zhi*.
It is certainly indispensable that these be included in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*);
let the gentleman examine them closely. 13.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yuanjing of Shishisi Temple in Xizhou. The Śramaṇa Shi Yuanjing was a native of Lin County in Fenzhou.
Leaving home at an early age, he devoted his mind to the lecture halls of the Xianshou school and attained realization of the esoteric purports of the various sutras.
He frequently visited Shishi Temple on Mount Miaolou in Xizhou, Pingyang Prefecture.
He preached the Dharma for the masses according to their conditions.
One day, he arrived at the Tile Kiln Slope by the North Gate and constructed a small hermitage by excavating the earth.
He was like a swallow dwelling in silence within its nest;
suddenly he addressed his disciples, saying, "I am about to return.
The assembly asked him for the date.
He replied, "It shall be tomorrow.
Rising at dawn, he bathed, changed into his three robes,
burned incense, sat in the lotus posture, recited a verse, and passed away.

14. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zuzhu of Mount Hua in Suzhou. Chapter Fourteen: The Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zuzhu of Mount Hua in Suzhou. Zuzhu’s courtesy name was Huanyi; Luting was his style name.
A native of Dantu.
His surname was Yang.
His mother, Lady Zhu, had a dream.
The bhikṣu Fan entered his room;
upon awakening, he gave birth to Daoshi.
From a young age, Daoshi was grave and reserved, having no craving for worldly affairs.
He delighted in performing Buddha-works.
At the age of thirteen, his parents sent him away to enter Longpan Mountain,
where he relied upon Master Chaoyang to receive the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other major Mahāyāna scriptures.
He received the tonsure at seventeen and full ordination at nineteen.
He thoroughly mastered the great meanings of the various sutras and said to himself:
Realizing that the basis of consciousness was unrelated to the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi),
he took up his staff and traveled to Shaoshi,
where he relied upon Master Dazhang for five years; subsequently, he went to Funiu, where he relied upon Master Gaoyuan for twelve summer retreats.
Having received the seal of approval from his two former teachers,
he subsequently traveled to the capital to visit the two Dharma Masters Song and Xiu,
from whom he fully mastered the essential tenets of the Qingliang tradition.
Hu Geshi of Huai'an invited him to reside at Bocishan,
where he commissioned the production of the Tripitaka and organized a Water-Land Unrestricted Assembly (Wuluzhai).
Upon arriving in Nanjing, he visited Master Wuji, where he served as the Second Seat.
During intervals between striking the *gandi*, he would enter the assembly to perform communal labor.
Upon completing these tasks, he traveled to Wanshou Temple in Jingkou to expound his Great Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
When he reached the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter, the earth quaked and the heavens rained down ambrosial jewel flowers.
At that time, Wuji led his followers to join him;
Miaofeng Chengyin and two other Chan monks also sat at his feet.
From then on, his reputation for the Way flourished, and the monastic communities looked up to him with deep admiration.
The Master honored the wise and humbled himself before the lowly,
just like the monk Never-Disparaging. He tirelessly exhorted and guided others,
establishing monasteries wherever he went.
When the Master was expounding the Forty-eight Vows,
there was a strange man wearing a white crown with snakes upon it.
Four-legged creatures came to listen to the preaching of the Dharma.
People marveled at this and questioned him.
He replied:
I was wearing my dharma cap when I suddenly lost sight of the landscape before me.
In the Jia-shen year of the Wanli era, I rested my staff at the foot of Lotus Peak in Su.
He constructed a vihāra and resided there.
On the ninth month of the Dinghai year, he suddenly manifested illness and addressed the assembly, saying:
On the twenty-second day, there shall be no dispersal;
you may then once again unfold the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
However, this old monk cannot bend to the whims of human sentiment.
At dawn on that day, he arose and bathed.
Sitting in the full lotus posture, he recited this verse:
"Space has neither face nor form."
Where there is no fixed position, one forcibly imposes an arrangement;
whether it be the "critical phrase" or not the "critical phrase," everywhere is the Tathāgata.
He spoke again, saying,
"This year I am sixty-six;
I do not know what I shall do."
Eh! All you people, fix your eyes and look at this news:
even the Buddhas and Patriarchs have arrived.
He used them without attachment;
having finished speaking, he passed away.
A wondrous fragrance lingered for a long time without dispersing.
The entire body was enshrined for three days;
his countenance remained as if he were alive.
He was cremated, and his remains were collected and enshrined in a stupa on the northern slope of Lotus Peak.
He lived to the age of sixty-six and had been ordained for fifty-four years.
King Shi Zhen composed an inscription for him.

Section Four: Clarifying the Meaning, Part Two of Four. The Biographies of Four Masters, with Six Others Included. 1. Biography of the Śramaṇa Minglong of Xiufeng Hermitage on Mount Yang in Beizhi. Biography of the Śramaṇa Minglong of Xiufeng Hermitage on Mount Yang in Beizhi: Daguang Minglong was the son of the Yao family of Suqian, Huainan. He was a man of great brilliance. From his youth, he possessed a profound aspiration for the Way. At the age of twenty-one, he left home to become a monk under the guidance of Master Daoyuan at Xiangshan Temple in Suzhou. He studied the Vinaya and the Abhidharma extensively. Later, he traveled to the capital, where he resided at Longhua Temple. There, he encountered the Chan Master Wumen, from whom he received the mind-seal. Subsequently, he visited various masters to resolve his remaining doubts. Eventually, he settled at Xiufeng Hermitage on Mount Yang in Beizhi, where he lived in seclusion and devoted himself to the practice of meditation. His reputation spread far and wide, and disciples gathered from all quarters. He passed away in the spring of the second year of the Yongzheng era (1724) at the age of sixty-nine. His remains were interred on the mountain. His dharma heirs include Master Shouyuan and others. [End of Biography] 1. Biography of the Śramaṇa Minglong of Xiufeng Hermitage on Mount Yang in Beizhi.The following is a list of rules that governs the application of the *karmadhāraya* compound formation (*samāsa*) in Pāṇini’s grammar, specifically concerning the treatment of the first member (*pūrvapada*) when it ends in the vowel *i*. These rules detail how the final *i* is replaced by *ī* (*ītvam*) under specific conditions. **1. General Rule:** The substitution of *ī* occurs after the word *purohita*, provided that it is followed by a word denoting a *gotra* (lineage). > *purohitādibhyo yañ-vidhau gotre* (P. 6.2.19) **2. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zhenjie of Qixia Temple in Yingtian. The Śramaṇa Shi Zhenjie of Qixia Temple in Yingtian, number two, whose style name was Suanan, was a monk.
He was a native of Xiangyang.
In his youth, he served as a student at the local commandery school.
Suddenly, the latent roots [of his awakening] sprouted within him, whereupon he took leave of his kin and severed his ties of affection.
Li Mingxiu had his hair shaved by Master Heshang.
Thereafter, he traveled north to the capital,
where he visited various lecture halls to study under different masters.
Residing under the tutelage of Master Juxiu, he satiated himself with the joy of the Dharma and deeply received the seal of Xianshou.
The Master’s learning was rich in both the inner and outer teachings;
every quarter consistently ranked him among the "dragons and elephants" of the Buddhist community.
After a long time, he took up his staff and traveled south to return to Jinling.
He emerged as the presiding master of Qixia on Mount She,
where his followers exceeded three hundred and his teachings encompassed the five vehicles.
Having occupied the lion throne and struck the great Dharma drum for over thirty years,
he cleared land from his surplus offerings to construct a monastery.
At that time, Minister Yin obtained an image of the Great Being from Langya.
Lord Lu Wutai also cast a golden image,
which he entirely offered to the Master for veneration;
the Vice Minister Luo inscribed the temple with the name "Circumambulation Hall" (Yuantong Jing-she).
The scholar Li Shilu of Jujing formed a "foreign friendship" with the Master.
In expounding the Great Dharma, he did not set fixed time limits.
Once, while lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he reached the chapter on the Many-Jeweled Stupa.
Suddenly, a jeweled stupa appeared before the seat, exactly as described in the sutras.
The fourfold assembly gazed upon it with rapt attention, filled with wonder at such a rare sight.
An imperial envoy named Zhang arrived, having received the command of Empress Dowager Cisheng, to witness this sacred omen together with them.
Thereupon, he brought forth a set of saṃghāṭī robes made of gold thread from the Imperial Armory and bestowed them upon him by imperial decree.
He then constructed a stūpa to the west of the lecture hall to commemorate this divine transformation.
Wang Daoqun recorded this account.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Mingde of Dongchan Temple in Jiaxing. The Śramaṇa Shi Mingde of Dongchan Temple in Jiaxing was styled Yueting; his courtesy name was Haomiao, and his pen-name was Jue. He hailed from Sanbai Stream.
Because he succeeded Chan Master Wansong Lin as his dharma heir, he was also known as Qiansong (Thousand Pines).
He was the son of the Zhou family from Wucheng in Huzhou.
From birth, he was exceptionally gifted and stood out as truly extraordinary.
In his childhood, while following his father into the Xizi Monastery,
he pointed to a painting of arhats on the wall and asked his father,
"Are these monks or laypeople?"
The father said, "He is a monk.
The Master sighed deeply and said,
"I wish to become one such as him."
Thereupon, he sought earnestly to leave the household life,
but his parents would not permit it.
When he reached the age of thirteen, he finally entered the Qingshan Hermitage at Shuanglin in the commandery.
He studied the teachings of Yoga under Seng Zhenxiang.
After four years had passed, he shaved his head;
hearing that there was a matter of "going beyond," he first went to attend upon Master Baichuan Hai.
Finding no resonance there,
he traveled alone in a single robe and straw sandals to visit various monastic assemblies,
crawling on his hands and knees to seek instruction and enduring every hardship.
Reflecting that his own karmic conditions for encountering Prajñā were meager,
he intended to travel to India to offer earnest supplications to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, praying to meet an enlightened master.
On his way through Central India, he encountered various circumstances.
Upon hearing that Wansong was preaching the Dharma, he went first to pay his respects.
Wansong asked him,
"Virtuous One, where have you come from, and what do you seek?"
He replied,
"I wish to knock at the Universal Gate to seek a true guide.
Song held up one finger and said:

The Master wept and bowed again, seeking a resolution regarding the great matter of birth and death.
Song said:

you must understand that there is no attachment to birth and death before you can succeed.
Upon hearing this, the Master was left speechless.
Relying on his full ordination,
[the Master] attended him morning and evening for a long time without making any progress. Finally,
out of necessity, Song transmitted to him the essential meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent effort to his studies until he reached the passage:
"How is it that from this state of pure essence, suddenly mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise?
At that moment, he was struck with sudden clarity, like clouds dispersing across the vast sky while the cold moon shines alone in brilliance.
He then composed a verse and presented it, saying:
Within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* there is originally no sūtra;

In the sixth month, the blazing sky is as hot as fire;

Since you have already awakened to the teachings of the Vehicle,

by means of this, the great matter beyond can be clarified.
While residing at Mount Jing,

Once, while walking among the forest foothills, he encountered a tiger crouching across his path.
The Master struck his monk’s staff on the ground and stepped forward;
the tiger fled.
He once read through the *Zaoboge lun* (Treatise on the Combined Exegesis) up to the "Ten Stages" chapter.

"From the very beginning there has been nothing;

Not only was my Way about to be propagated,

Before long, Song passed away.
The Master hung his cauldron and guarded the stupa for three years.
Hearing of the flourishing lectures at the seat of the Dharma Master Fohui of Jiyuan, he donned a bamboo hat and went to join him.
Jiyuan, too, silently recognized his worth and held him in high esteem.
His disciple Shaquan was quite conceited and did not rely on his master’s reputation.
The Master consequently hung up his staff at Baosian Temple.
Baosian was but a few inches away from Fohui.
Therefore, in the morning he carried his almsbowl;
at noon he listened to the lectures;
and in the evening, together with more than ten fellow practitioners, he expounded upon their essential meanings and principles.
Thereupon, the number of people increased day by day until the incense offerings could no longer be sustained.
The Master secretly prayed to the deity of the monastery, saying:
"If I am destined to have a karmic affinity with the Holy Teaching..."
The deity was not parsimonious and provided protection.
After some time, a non-Buddhist practitioner came from between the clouds and offered one hundred *shi* of rice.
From then on, the abundance of his rewards surpassed even that of the Buddha’s wisdom.
On the day of the opening of the hall, Jiyuan ordered an attendant monk to present him with his robe and whisk;
he declined them and returned them.
He offered a single incense stick, which was presented by Wansong.
Thereafter, he went alone back to Mount Lingxiao at Jingshan.
Because his "obstructing blockage" remained unbroken, he again applied himself to intensive study for three years.
One night, during the first watch, he sat in meditation with legs crossed.
Suddenly, his mind and its objects merged in profound stillness, and his doubts and obstructions were dissolved like melting ice.
He then leaped up and uttered this verse:
"The green bamboo of a thousand years, the pine of ten thousand years."
Leaf by leaf, branch by branch, this is the ancestral wind;
Cloudy peaks and lofty summits are the dwelling places of the hidden ones.
In wordless radiance, the bright sun is universally the same for all.
He hurried to the Wansong Pagoda and said,
"The old man has not deceived me. From then on,
his reputation for the Way flourished even more, and students flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel.
Diplomatic envoys arrived from the four quarters every day of the year without fail.

Sengche, Kongtian, and their ilk glared at him with contempt and dared not approach;
they ultimately slandered the Master with unfathomable matters.
Before the day was out, the truth was revealed, and Kongtian sat in disgrace for his false accusations and fled.

The Master traveled south to Chicheng,
where those among the non-Buddhists who converted to the faith were beyond counting.

"You were a lion in the past; are you a child now?

The Master said:
The Sage established his teachings truly as a means to draw those lost on the path toward awakening.
To claim that by mentioning any single dharma, all six are thereby present, is to speak only of conventional truth and result in frivolous proliferation.
What more need be said of the learner?
As for the preceding five [stages], let them be set aside and not discussed.
As it is said: "Ultimate, ultimate—then all is ultimately so."
Like gold extracted from ore,
or like a jade disc separated from its raw matrix;
for this reason, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he contemplated the nine realms.
All sentient beings attain Buddhahood simultaneously.
It is not merely that the primary retributions (*pratyātmabhāva*) of the nine realms are the entirety of Vairocana;
rather, since the nine realms' environmental retributions (*bhājanaloka*) are also non-other than the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), there is nothing that is not this land.
Therefore, it is praised, saying:
"How marvelous! Sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata;
yet, due to deluded thoughts, they do not realize them for themselves."

If it is indeed as you say,
then those who are like dung beetles will never have a day of attaining Buddhahood.
Among all sentient beings, not a single one has given rise to the bodhicitta.
That is to say, the ten dharma realms are all but a single troop of iron hammers without holes.
Even if one were to say that a dung beetle could ultimately achieve Buddhahood, it would be impossible.
"If the Tathāgata were to become deluded again on some day and turn back into a sentient being, with his gold becoming as heavy as ore once more—

Since this is the case for one realm, so it is for all.
This is true for all realms in general; however,

"Why must you trouble yourself with whether he has attained Buddhahood or not?
The Master laughed and said,
"You would go on to become a thoroughgoing dung beetle."
Those who heard him did not fail to hold his discourse in high esteem.

such that even bhikṣus would don their saṃghāṭī robes to pay him homage.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Śākyamuni Jiaoheng of Qingshou Monastery in the Yan Capital, Part Two. The śramaṇa Śākyamuni Jiaoheng, whose courtesy name was Xuming, was a disciple of Puzhao Bao. His secular surname was Li, and he was a native of Changping County in Bingzhou. From his youth, he possessed a sharp and penetrating intellect; at the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under the guidance of the Venerable Master Wenzhen of Huayan Monastery in the capital. At fifteen, he received full ordination from the Venerable Master Daoyuan of the same monastery. Subsequently, he traveled to various regions to study the teachings, eventually arriving at the Dharma seat of the Venerable Master Puzhao Bao of Qinglong Monastery in the capital. There, he served as an attendant for three years, during which time he thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries of the scriptures and commentaries, and exhaustively mastered the essential doctrines of the various schools. He was particularly adept at lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*. Later, he resided at Qinglong Monastery, where he propagated the Dharma extensively. In the second year of the Zhenghe era (1112), he was invited by imperial decree to reside at Qingshou Monastery in the Yan Capital. During the winter of that year, he fell ill and passed away on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month. He was sixty-one years of age. The Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Dingguang" (Fixed Light). His remains were interred within the monastery grounds. His disciples erected a stele to record his life, and the eminent monk Zongyue composed the inscription. It is said that when the Master was about to pass away, he told his disciples: "I have been living in this world for over sixty years. My life has been one of diligent cultivation, and I have never committed even a single transgression. Now, my end has come. You should all strive to maintain the precepts and cultivate yourselves with diligence. Having spoken thus, he closed his eyes and passed away peacefully. His funeral rites were conducted according to the prescribed protocols. His disciples enshrined his remains in a stupa within the monastery. His writings include commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, as well as several other works, totaling over ten fascicles. His secular surname was Wei. He was a man of extraordinary character and profound insight. From his youth, he possessed a natural affinity for the Way; he was diligent in his studies and deeply committed to the practice of meditation. He traveled extensively through various regions, seeking out and attending upon eminent masters. His reputation spread far and wide, drawing disciples from all quarters. Huiyuan, however, remained steadfast in his resolve, never wavering in his pursuit of the ultimate truth. He resided at Mount Lingyan, where he established a center for the propagation of the teachings.

His moral integrity was such that even wild beasts would not harm him, and birds would often gather to listen to his sermons. Huiyuan was renowned for his mastery of both exoteric and esoteric doctrines. He was particularly skilled in the interpretation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*. His lectures were so eloquent and profound that they inspired awe in those who heard them. He was also a master of the Vinaya, ensuring that his disciples lived in accordance with the precepts. Throughout his life, Huiyuan remained dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings. He frequently engaged in acts of charity, providing for the needy and the destitute. His compassion extended even to the smallest creatures, and he was known for his gentle and patient demeanor. When he preached, his voice was clear and resonant, capable of reaching even the most distant listeners. In his later years, Huiyuan retired to a secluded hermitage on the slopes of Mount Lingyan. There, he devoted himself entirely to meditation and contemplation, seeking to realize the nature of reality. He passed away peacefully, surrounded by his disciples, at the age of seventy-two. His remains were interred on the mountain, where a stupa was erected in his honor. To this day, his legacy endures as a testament to the power of faith, wisdom, and compassion. *** I have seen the walls of Master Yuan. The Śramaṇa Shi Daoyuan of Zhaojue Temple in Chengdu, the thirteenth [entry], was styled Ch’ean (Chè’ān). His secular surname was Liang. He was born in the village of Shuangfeng, Xiangyang County, Jingzhou. From childhood he possessed a profound nature and a sharp intelligence. At age twelve, he entered the monastery of Zhongxing in his hometown to become a monk under the Venerable Huiming. He received the full precepts at age twenty. He was diligent in his studies and devoted himself to the practice of meditation. Later, he traveled to the capital, where he resided at the Chan Hall of the Great Xingshan Temple. There he encountered the Master Dajian, with whom he attained great realization. Subsequently, he traveled through various regions, visiting famous mountains and sacred sites. Eventually, he arrived at Zhaojue Temple in Chengdu, where he remained until his death. He was eighty-four years old. His remains were interred within the temple grounds. His dharma heirs were numerous, and his influence on the teaching was vast. Thus ends the biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Daoyuan. 13. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Daoyuan of Zhaojue Temple in Chengdu. Haiyin Long: Shi Huicai, whose style name was Foxin (Buddha-Mind). [The text continues with the biographical details of Shi Huicai. ...He resided at Shangfeng Monastery in Tanzhou. His dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Zhongfeng. Master Zhongfeng’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Dahui. Master Dahui’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Yuanwu. Master Yuanwu’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Foyan. Master Foyan’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Fenyang. Master Fenyang’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Yunmen. Master Yunmen’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Nanquan. Master Nanquan’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Mazu. Master Mazu’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Huairang. Master Huairang’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Huineng. Master Huineng’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Hongren. Master Hongren’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Daoxin. Master Daofu’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Hongren. Master Hongren’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from Master Bodhidharma. Master Bodhidharma’s dharma lineage was as follows: He received the dharma from the twenty-eighth Indian Patriarch, Master Prajñātāra. Thus, the transmission has been passed down from generation to generation, from India to China, reaching the present day. Shi Yunneng, whose courtesy name was Chengfu and religious name Chongzhen, was styled Huimù. He resided at Zhongyan Temple in Meizhou. His secular surname was Liang, and he was a native of the same region. From childhood, he possessed a sharp intellect and a profound disposition for the Way. At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk under the guidance of the Venerable Daoyuan of Xiangshan Temple in Chengdu. He received full ordination at the age of twenty and diligently applied himself to the study of the Vinaya. Subsequently, he traveled extensively through various regions, visiting and paying homage to all the eminent masters of the time. Later, he returned to his native land and settled at Zhongyan Temple. There, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of meditation and the cultivation of the mind, remaining aloof from worldly affairs. His demeanor was serene and dignified, and his spiritual power was such that it moved both the common people and the officials. During the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong summoned him to the capital, where he was treated with great honor. After several years, he requested leave to return to his hometown, and the Emperor granted his request. Upon his arrival, the local governor and the entire populace welcomed him with offerings and prostrations. He remained at the temple until his death, never leaving. He passed away at the age of seventy-four in the second year of the Tianbao era. The Emperor issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him the posthumous title "Great Master Chongzhen" and the honorific "Virtuous Monk. A stele was erected at the temple to commemorate him. His remains were interred within the temple grounds. His disciples numbered over two hundred, among whom the most prominent were the Venerable Huiming of Qingcheng Mountain and the Venerable Huishou of Mount Emei. Both were men of great virtue and learning who continued his lineage. 11. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yunneng of Zhongyan Temple in Meizhou. 11. Dao rebuked him, saying,
"Do not err."
Thereupon, he withdrew for three years of retreat;
only then did he receive the former instructions.
He entered Min Province to visit Zhuan-an at Gushan Mountain, where he paid his respects and sought instruction.
When National Teacher [Huai] asked, "What is the meaning of the phrase 'not crossing the stone gate'?
Zhuan-an replied instantly, "Idle words."
He attained sudden enlightenment upon hearing these words.
Later, a monk asked him,
"What is the true person of no station?"
Sheng said:
"I have heard that one may be wealthy and noble in life, yet become poor after death.
Shi Huiwen, surnamed Lu'an, was born into the Zheng family in Fuzhou.
He resided together with Sheng at Zhuan-an in the east;
not long after, because Zhuan-an retired from his duties,
he [Sheng] took charge himself.
Yet, my mind remained unsettled.
I subsequently visited the venerable elders Gao’an Wuxin, Nanhua Ming, and Caotang Qing,
all of whom appreciated my potential.
When Zhuan-an moved to Qianyuan in Min,
Wen returned to visit him. An said,
"The arising of emotion creates a barrier to wisdom."
The manifestations of thought differ;
do not let your intelligence stagnate in confinement.
Bring forth a single phrase of the Way.
Wen was suddenly enlightened and presented this verse:
"Pressed out until my whole body is a mouth, what harm is there in reviling the rain and scolding the wind?
Last night, a fierce tiger in the village ahead bit to death a great beast of the South Mountain."
Zhuan-an approved of him.
Later, he resided at Langshan in Tongzhou and,
together with Sheng, raised the red banner of Zhuan-an, serving as an excellent guide for the region.
