Yongshi was a native of Mianzhou.
From an early age, he possessed the spiritual roots of enlightenment and was able to sever his attachments;
casting off the shackles of desire, he was like a fish escaping from a net.
Entering the Garden of Dharma was like a phoenix perching upon a catalpa tree.
At nineteen, he passed the scriptural examination and received a certificate of ordination from the ancestral temple.
After donning the dyed robes, he first explored the Vinaya school.
Having rectified his transgressions and maintained his observances— like a flawless white jade or a fine gem—
he immersed himself in the ocean of the teachings for five years before crossing the pass and traveling south.
As he traveled among the fourfold assembly, all recognized him as a man of exceptional talent;
he visited eminent masters everywhere until,
upon entering Longmen, he happened to be walking along the corridors.
Upon seeing an image of a foreigner on a wall painting, he suddenly attained realization.

That evening, he informed Gao’an, who recited a verse by Fayan: The Great Way is not difficult; It simply avoids picking and choosing. Avoid picking and choosing, and there is nothing left out; If you pick and choose, you will fall into the weeds.
On his head he wore a marten-fur hat, and at his waist he hung a horn-tipped dagger.
His speech was such that no one could understand it;
it required someone to interpret it for him.
Dongshan struck the fire-drill with a stick and showed it to him, saying,
"I have finished translating for you.
At these words, Yuan attained great enlightenment and presented this verse:
The sounds and languages of foreign lands are inexhaustible;
beneath Qiyun Pavilion, they are all simultaneously understood.
The gateway of the mouth is vast and boundless.
He swallowed the "thorny chestnut" of Yangqi.
Gaowan sent him to serve Foyan.
Foyan said:
"My Way shall spread to the East.
Shi Shanneng was also a Dharma heir of Ga’ān;
his clan was from Yǎnglíng, though his surname remains unknown.
One day, Ga’ān was performing communal labor (fushō) and selecting vegetables.
Next-ān, knowing that Neng’s karmic conditions were ripe, suddenly threw a cat into Neng’s arms.
As Neng hesitated, [Next-ān struck him].
Beopan thrust him against his chest and kicked him down;
he attained sudden great enlightenment and rose, sighing and laughing.
Having served him for a long time, his virtuous fragrance spread far and wide.
The clergy and laity alike turned their hearts toward him, and he emerged surrounded by devas and humans.
He resided as abbot at Zhongji Temple in Fuzhou, greatly propagating the school’s teachings;
the world called him the "Dharma Banner beneath the Twin Trees."
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture, Part Three. Shi Yanchong, whose style name was Kentang, was a śramaṇa at Jingci Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture.
He was the son of the Sheng family from Yushan in Hangzhou.
From his youth, his wisdom-nature was bright and radiant, and his roots of goodness were firmly established within him.
He understood from birth that he must seek liberation from the bonds of the mundane world.
He then followed the explanations of the Mingkongyuan (Court of Luminous Emptiness) and became qualified for tonsure.
Having studied the Vinaya for five summer retreats,
he traveled alone with a single alms bowl and went directly to the Great Hall of Dàyuǎn of Dàyú Hóngzhì.
Later, he heard Monk Ju Donglin address the assembly, saying:
"In this place of mine, there is nothing else particularly profound or mysterious;
there is only vegetable-stalk soup and rice with iron nails."
"Let it be as you wish to chew upon it.
Yan secretly rejoiced at this and went directly to present his views and understanding.
Donglin said to him:
The very place where you perceive is precisely sitting within the mirror-like awareness.
Yanguan, cast aside everything you have previously acquired all at once;
focus your mind with single-minded diligence and investigate it thoroughly.
One day, hearing a neighboring monk cite Nanquan’s saying, “When people see this single stalk of flowers,
it is like being in a dream,” he suddenly awakened within himself and said silently,
“Striking the grass is only intended to startle the snake.”
The next day,入室 (入室) went into Donglin’s quarters and asked,
“Where was it that Yantou secretly revealed his meaning?
Yan said:
"Today I have captured this old thief.
Lin said,
"The life of Master Bodhidharma is in your hands."
As Yan was about to open his mouth, Lin suddenly struck him a punch to the chest.
Instantly, Yan attained great enlightenment; sweat poured down his back as he nodded his head and said:
Linji said, "Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not much more than this.
How could these words have been empty?
He presented a verse, saying:
If one is to act as a human being, one must act with thoroughness;
if one is to kill, one must see blood.
Thus it was with Deshan and Yantou.
"A single iron bar ten thousand *li* long.
Lin Shen approved of this. 4.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zhenci of Zhiye Monastery in Wuzhou. The Śramaṇa Shi Zhenci of Zhiye Monastery in Wuzhou, number four. Shi Zhenci’s style name was Yu’ān.
He was the son of the Li family of Tongchuan.
From his childhood, he aspired to the state of emptiness and tranquility and delighted in visiting monasteries.

He earnestly requested permission from his parents to rely upon the Zhengfayuan Monastery in Chengdu, where he shaved his head, received full ordination, and took the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Pure and austere as ice and snow, his wisdom shone like the rising sun.

Devoted to the study of the *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures, he traveled extensively among lecture halls to listen to the exposition of the *Niyatāniyatagati-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Definitive and Indefinite) of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
When the four great elements have each departed, where then would this deluded body be? Ultimately it has no substance; in reality, it is identical to an illusion or a transformation.
Thereupon, he had an awakening and composed a verse, which says:
"A single bright pearl."
Here with me, as soon as you touch it or move it,
light is emitted and the earth shakes.
I presented this to the various lecturers,
but none were able to identify it; thus,
I returned to present it to my preceptor.
The Master tested him with the koan regarding the dog having no Buddha-nature.
Cizhao said,
"Of the hundreds of thousands of public cases, none surpass this verse."
The Master then rebuked him and expelled him.
Thereupon, he traveled south to Mount Lu, where he hung his staff at Yuan Tong.
At that time, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Abbot and was conducting the "entering the room" (入室) interviews for the assembly.
A monk asked Yunmen,
"When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha,
what then? Yunmen said:
"The Buddha is also a dust-mote.
Upon hearing this, Ci opened up in sudden enlightenment and,
following the sound of these words, let out a shout.
Pointing his finger at his chest, he said,
"The Buddha is also a defilement.
He then presented this verse:
"Brushing away the dust to see the Buddha—the Buddha is also dust.
When the question is resolved, the answer is resolved; turn your body directly beneath you.
I urge you to drink one more cup of wine.
"Once you have passed the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friends.
Furthermore, he offered this verse on the Samādhi of Every Dust-Mote:
"Rice in the bowl; water in the bucket."
A rare jewel sits apart at the bottom of the Kunlun Abyss;
a single speck of dust ascends and races atop Mount Sumeru.
The clear-eyed Persian laughs and snaps his fingers.
With a smile, he snapped his fingers, and a pure breeze arose from atop the coral branches.
Wan’an nodded in approval.
Thereupon, his fame spread throughout the four quarters and his Way harmonized with all paths.
The Master of Wisdom emerged to instruct and guide his disciples;
he was truly a great hand for slaying dragons. 5.

Biography of the Śramaṇa An Yong of Gushan, Fuzhou. The biography of the Śramaṇa An Yong of Gushan, Fuzhou, number five. An Yong of Fuzhou, whose style name was Mugwan (Wood Hermitage), was a śramaṇa.
He was the son of the Wu family of Min County.
From birth, he possessed the innate nature of the Way; his conduct was solemn and dignified.
Though his body was immersed in the entanglements of worldly affection, his mind harbored aspirations for the transcendent.
Having tonsured his hair at the age of twenty, he set his lofty standards beyond the mundane world.
Hearing that there was the Way of the Separate Transmission,
he went to visit Chan Master Lan’an at Yunmen.
Upon entering the room, Zhaozhou looked back and asked,
"Without asking about words, and without asking about wordlessness.
The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while.
He was not permitted to remain for long in the assembly before the World-Honored One;
immediately thereafter,
he let out a shout and suddenly attained eternal, instantaneous enlightenment.
"All you people who have not yet attained an entrance must attain an entrance.
Once you have attained an entrance, you must not forget this old monk.
Yong said:
"How thick-skinned you are to speak like that!
Mudan does not say it this way:
if you people have not yet attained an entrance, you must attain an entrance."
"Once you have attained this point of entry, you must immediately cast it aside; only then will you succeed.
All the Dharma he preached was as concise and clear as this.
At that time, there was a master named Anfen.
In his youth, he and Yong served together as scribes in An-guo.
Later, Yong departed to rely upon Lan’an, but they did not reach a spiritual accord;
thus, [Foyin] took his leave and went to pay his respects to Dahui at Mount Jing.
While traveling along the banks of the Qiantang River,
he gazed up at the imperial palace and suddenly heard the street patrol shout, "The Minister comes!
At that moment, he attained great enlightenment and spoke this verse:
For many years this matter has hung upon my breast;
I have questioned all quarters of the land, yet my eyes remain unopened.
Now, at this moment, both liver and gall are rent asunder.
At the sound of "The Minister comes upon the river," he returned to Xichan.
Lan’an welcomed him and bestowed upon him the kāṣāya robe.
From then on, he did not plan for a permanent residence;
later, he lived in a hermitage at Jianmen,
where his transformative influence spread throughout the regions south of the mountains.
Students followed him. 6.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Tanmi of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture. The sixth [section]: The Śramaṇa Shi Tanmi, styled Hunyuan, was a resident of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture.
He was the son of the Lu family of Tiantai.
From birth, he was exceptionally brilliant and gifted, far surpassing ordinary men.
Having lost his father’s protection in childhood, his aspirations were lofty and transcendent.
Initially, he relied on Zifu Temple in Yiyang to investigate the teachings of India.
At sixteen, he received full ordination and entered the register of the Great Sangha;
his mastery of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Vinaya collections was so refined that it was entirely without flaw.
He studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school with great diligence,

until he understood the principles of sudden and gradual, partial and perfect, and the inherent nature of reality— the "poison of principle"— as clearly as pointing at something in the palm of his hand.
One day, he sighed and said:
The subtlety of the teachings and vehicles is beyond all description;
yet, as long as one does not transcend names and words, one will ultimately fail to see one's true nature.
It would be better to change one's robes and follow the study of the separate transmission.
If there were an opportunity to see him, it would bring joy to my entire life.
Hearing that Dahui was preaching the Way at Mount Jingshan,
I packed my belongings and went there to pay my respects.
He also visited Xuechao Yi, Ciyuan, Yuan, and others,
yet none of them elicited any awakening or realization.
Thereupon, he traveled from Min to Quannan.
He entered the service of Master Zhongguang and was appointed to the position of *weina*. There,
he heard Master Zhong recount the karmic incident of Xiangyan striking the bamboo.
Suddenly attaining enlightenment, he presented a verse;
when Zhong questioned him about Xuan Sha’s remark that [the master] had not yet reached the ultimate,
his responses were unhindered.
He first entrusted him with these words:
"Only after this may you see Mahāmati.
Thereupon, having received these instructions, he took his leave and departed for Mei-yang.
He served with diligence for four years;
Hui once ascended the seat [to preach].
Upon leaving the world, he received an imperial decree to serve as abbot of Jingci Temple, where he widely propagated the Way of Loyalty through the Teachings.
His outdoor sandals were always kept full.
He passed away, and his stupa was erected at the northwestern corner of his home mountain.
**Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xianjie of Tiantong Monastery in Mingzhou** The Śramaṇa Shi Xianjie of Tiantong Monastery in Mingzhou, whose style name was Miman, was... [Biography continues].
He was the son of the Zheng family in Fuzhou.
His mother dreamed that an elderly monk from Mount Lu entered her residence, and she subsequently gave birth to the Master.
From childhood, he was exceptionally gifted and surpassed others.
Upon reaching maturity, he shaved his head, received full ordination, and traveled extensively to visit various spiritual mentors.
Finally, he went to pay his respects to Master Ying’an Hua at Mingguo Hermitage in Quzhou.
One day, the Master asked him:
"What is the Eye of the True Dharma?
He replied,
"A broken sand pot."
Ying'an nodded in agreement and spoke a verse, saying:
"The phrase of great penetration that accords with the occasion."
When the top of the head is opened wide and revealed,
we have followed this path for four years now;
though interrogated and examined, there is not a trace to be found.
Although he had not yet been entrusted with the robe and bowl,
his spirit and bearing swallowed up heaven and earth;
he instead took up the Eye of the True Dharma.
He was called "Broken Sand Pot.
Later, he went forth to reside at Wugu Hermitage in Quzhou,
and subsequently moved to Huazang Monastery on Mount Jiangshan in Xiangfu.
Not long thereafter, he received an imperial decree to preside over Mount Jing and Lingyin Monasteries.
He ascended the hall and said: "Oxhead expounds horizontally and vertically, yet he does not know there is the pivotal bolt of the higher realm."
There are some people who are like lacquered buckets, unable to distinguish east from west or south from north.
When asked, "What is the pivotal bolt that turns things upward? how is this any different from urinating on one's bed while wide awake?
I have a turning phrase for you.
It is neither upward nor downward;
the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands searches for it but cannot find it.
Today, this old monk bestows it upon the great assembly.
After a long silence, he said,
"Master Bodhidharma had no front teeth. Then,
ascending the hall, he struck his staff upon the ground and said:
"When deluded, one is deluded only regarding this very thing.
He then struck the ground once and said,
"When awakened, one awakens only regarding this very thing."
When delusion and awakening are both forgotten,
one adds further refuse to a heap of discarded rags.
Is there anyone who can utter a single phrase from the state where the total function is uniquely liberated— where the east surges up and the west sinks down?
"If you cannot say it, I shall say it myself," he said,
and casting down his staff, he remarked,
"Thirty years from now, I shall raise this again."
Master Jinfeng addressed the assembly, saying:
"Twenty years ago, this old monk possessed a grandmotherly heart;
twenty years later, I am without such a grandmotherly heart."
[The monk asked,] "Regarding the monastic community, what is the Master’s compassionate heart toward sentient beings?
Feng said:
The questioner asked an ordinary question and received an ordinary answer; the Master answered as a Sage would answer a Sage.
The assembly then asked:
"What is the Master’s lack of a 'grudging heart' (wú lǎopó xīn)?"
Feng said, "When asked about the ordinary, do not answer with the ordinary; when asked about the sacred, do not answer with the sacred.
The Master said:
If I had seen him speaking like that at the time,
I would have told him:
"If you yourself can let go of it."
Naturally, one does not fall into this pitfall of the holy and the profane.
Again, having finished citing the story of the old woman burning the hermitage, the Master said:
"Many in the monastic communities have offered comments and evaluations on this koan."
Today this old monk has torn his own face;
he cannot help but admit his defeat before the assembly.
He must certainly have all quarters examine this matter clearly.
He then summoned the assembly and said:
"This old woman’s dwelling is deep and secure, impenetrable as a sealed vessel;
yet she persistently scatters flowers upon withered wood."
Flames burst forth from within the cold crags;
this monk stands solitary and towering, accustomed to entering the surging waves.
At ease, he cuts off the surging tide of heaven.
In truth, not even a drop has arisen from within.
Examine this closely:
while there is certainly no lack of shackles and fetters to be struck upon when things are brought forth, [the root cause remains absent].
If you say that both [you and I] have not yet even dreamed of the Buddha-dharma,
where does the ultimate meaning of this old monk’s current way of holding it up lead?
After a long silence, he said:
"A single tangle of willow threads cannot be gathered;
together with the mist, they lean against the jade balustrade.
He ascended the hall, struck the meditation staff upon the floor, and said:
To call the entire earth "one phrase" is to carry a cangue and wear shackles;
not to call it "one phrase" is for the karmic consciousness to be vast and unbounded.
To penetrate and transcend both extremes—this is liberation.
Having attained purity— naked, bare, and stark—
you must not sweep the entire Dharma school into oblivion.
Therefore, Master Yunmen said:
To exhaustively encompass the entire earth and heavens without the slightest flaw or affliction is still a "turning phrase.
To not see a single dharma is only half the presentation; one must further know that there is the "total presentation" as well.
The Master said:
"The sword has long since been lost;
you are merely marking the boat."
He held up his staff, struck it once, and descended from the seat. 8.

The Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Zuoxian of Mount Wolong in Kuizhou. The Śramaṇa Shi Zuoxian, whose style name was Po’an, was perfumed by the Eight Dharmas. His secular surname was... [text continues].
He was the son of Wang of Guang’an.
Having left home at a young age, he applied himself with vigor to the ancestral Way,
never finding restful sleep at night.
Carrying only a single robe with him,
he heard that Mida was greatly propagating the Linji school;
he thereupon packed his belongings in a cloth bag and went to pay his respects.
Mimang, recognizing that he was a vessel of great capacity, subjected him to intense prodding and pressure.
One day, while Mimang was ascending the hall to address the assembly,
[the monk] suddenly attained realization.
Later, when Miam resided at Lingyin Monastery,
he appointed the Master to share his seat.
One day, a certain practitioner asked him:
"When a monkey cannot be caught, what can be done?
The Master said,
"What is the use of trying to catch it?"
Just as wind blowing across water naturally forms patterns,
there was once a lecture master of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* who requested instruction.
The Master spoke a verse, saying:
"To see while still being separated from seeing is not true seeing;
when the eight returns are exhausted, there is nothing further to return to."
The trees have fallen, the autumn sky reveals the bare bones of the mountains;
who knows who can recognize the old Gautama?
At that time, Shitian Faxun came to attend the Master.
He questioned him by citing the story of the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa’s smile.
Xun replied:
"A scorched brick breaks through the ice right to its bottom."
"Red-Eye ran straight into a matchhead.
The Master nodded his approval.
Later, he emerged into the world as his dharma heir.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Chongyue of Lingyin Monastery in Lin’an Prefecture, Number Nine. The Śramaṇa Shi Chongyue, whose courtesy name was Songyuan, [was born...].
He was a native of the Wu family of Longquan in Chuzhou.
In the second year of the Longxing era, he received full ordination at the White Lotus Hermitage on West Lake in Hangzhou.
He spent the longest period of his life traveling to visit various masters.
Later, he visited Master Mitan Jie.
Hearing the master’s question in the meditation hall— “It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing”—
he suddenly attained great enlightenment and received the seal of the Dharma.
Because Mimian returned to Lingyin, he was appointed to the position of First Seat.
After some time, he entered the monastic world, first taking up residence at Chengzhao in Pingjiang,
followed by Guangxiao in Jiangyin, Jianfu in Raozhou, and Xiangshan in Mingzhou.
In the third year of the Qingyuan era of Emperor Ningzong, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Lingyin Monastery, where he remained for three cycles of winter and summer.
He then requested to retire in old age to the eastern hermitage of the monastery.
On the fourth day of the eighth month in the second year of the JiaTai era, he personally wrote a letter of farewell to the high officials and nobility.
He spoke these words to instruct his students, saying:
"There is a person of great power;
for what reason can they not lift their foot?"
He further said:
"The opening of the mouth does not reside on the tip of the tongue.
He entrusted his disciples with the solemn charge that the propagation of the Dharma was their primary duty.
He then wrote a verse, saying:
"In coming, there is no place from which one comes;
in going, there is no place to which one goes."
In a flash, he turned the mysterious pivot;
even Buddhas and Patriarchs were at a loss.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was seventy-one years of age and forty years since his ordination.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the plain of North Gaofeng.
Those who attained the Dharma were Xiangshan Guangmu and Yunju Shanka. 10.

Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Shifan of Mount Jing in Lin’an Prefecture. Shi Shifan, styled Wuzhun, was a śramaṇa of Mount Jing in Lin’an Prefecture. His biography is the tenth. Shi Shifan’s courtesy name was Wuzhun.
He was the son of the Yang family from Zizhong in Shu.
At the age of nine, he followed Master Daqin of Mount Yinping to enter the monastic life.
He could recite any text from memory after reading it only once.
In the sixth year of the Shaoxi era of the Southern Song dynasty, he began traveling with his robes tied at his waist to Chengdu’s Zhengfa Temple.
There, he requested instruction from Master Yao regarding the practice of seated meditation.
Yao said:
"What is Zen? Who is it that sits?
The Master then investigated this day and night.
One day, while using the toilet,
he attained a realization because of a previous conversation.
The following year, he traveled through Guangzhou and Zhejiang to pay his respects to Fozhao at Yuyang Monastery.
Zhao asked, "Where are you from?
He replied, "Jianzhou."
He asked again,
"Did you bring your sword?
The Master then gave a shout.
The Buddha-illuminator laughed and said,
"This fellow with the black head is acting recklessly.
The Master was poor and lacked the means to have his hair shaved."
His contemporaries called him "Wutouzi" (The Crow-Headed One).
While he was residing at Lingyin after breaking through [his attachments],
a certain practitioner once questioned Pó'ān as the Master was in attendance.
"How can one catch a young monkey?
What is to be done? Poyan said, "Why use catching at all?"
Just as wind blowing across water naturally forms ripples,
the Master attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words.
Not long after, he traveled with Master Shixi to Mount Tiantai and Mount Yandang.
At that time, Master Xuefeng Yun was residing at Ruiyan and had invited the Master to share his seat.
One night, he dreamed of a majestic figure who held a bundle of thatched grass and bestowed it upon him.
The following day, an envoy from Qingliang Temple in Mingzhou came to welcome the Master.
Upon entering the temple, he saw that the nameplate of the temple guardian deity was inscribed with the surname Mao;
moreover, the deity’s attire and headgear were no different from what he had seen in his dream.
He resided at [Mount] Jiao for three years and subsequently moved to Xuedou.
Later, by imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot of Ayuwang Monastery.
After a long period there, he was appointed to fill the vacancy at Shuangjing.
Before long, he was summoned into the inner palace to preach the Dharma at Xuzheng Hall;
his teachings pleased the Emperor, who bestowed upon him a golden brocade robe and conferred the title Chan Master Fojian.
The Master resided at Mount Jing.
The temple buildings were twice destroyed by fire,
yet both times they were restored anew.
Furthermore, forty *li* from the monastery, he constructed a hundred-pillared hall to receive wandering monks from all quarters.
He named the hall "Ten Thousand Years of Continuity.
Next, several hundred paces to its west,
he constructed a hermitage as a place for his final resting place.
Furthermore, he constructed a multi-storied pavilion upon it to enshrine the imperial calligraphy bestowed by the court.
The Master’s ancestors had resided in Shu;
however, encountering times of turmoil, their lineage was severed.
He then established a shrine in the mountains to offer sacrifices to his ancestors according to secular custom.
When the matter was reported to the court, he was granted the title "Yuanzhao" (Complete Illumination) to commemorate his filial devotion.
In the year Wushen of the Chunyou era of the Song dynasty, he built a residence on the banks of the Bright Moon Pond and inscribed it with the name "Retired Plowman.
On the first day of the third month of that same year, he fell ill.
He then ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying,
"This mountain monk is both old and ill;
I have no strength left to engage in idle chatter with you all."
Now, having exerted myself,
I shall thoroughly shake out everything that I have not previously been able to express before you all.
He then rose from his seat, shook out his robe, and said,
"How much is that?
He then returned to the abbot's quarters.
On the fifteenth day, he gathered his assembly and personally wrote a memorial and several dozen words of a farewell letter.
Yet, he conversed with his guests with laughter and jesting as if it were his usual routine.
When night fell, he wrote a verse, saying:
When coming, it is empty and hollow;
when going, one is stark naked.
If you wish to inquire further into the ultimate point:
At Tiantai there was a stone bridge;
he passed away after traveling for a short while.
His coffin remained enshrined for fourteen days.
His posthumous memorial was submitted to the throne.
The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow incense and coarse silk.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Yuanzhao Monastery.
11. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Daowu of Puzhao Temple in Zhengzhou. Attached: Baiyun Hai. The Śramaṇa Shi Daowu of Puzhao Temple in Zhengzhou was titled Foguang (Buddha-Light).
Guan was a native of Lanzhou in Shaanxi.
From the moment he was born, his teeth and hair grew fully developed, and he possessed the physical marks of a great man.
At the age of sixteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it.
He then fasted until he was nearly dead;
subsequently, he entered a temple in the village to shave his head.
After two years had passed, while staying overnight at a shop in Wanzi, Lin-tao, he dreamed of a Buddhist monk.
Shaking his voice, he called out to wake him, and suddenly heard the neighing of a horse.
He attained sudden, great enlightenment and was overcome with joy beyond measure.
He spoke a verse, saying:
"Jeyara, Jeyara! This very thing pervades all of space.
He then returned and told his mother, "I picked up an object along the way."
The mother asked, "What is it?
The Master replied,
"That which has not been seen since beginningless time."
The mother said,
"What joy is there in this?
She then took her leave, intending to travel to various regions.
The mother asked,
"Where are you going?
He replied:
Rivers must flow to the sea;
cranes emerge from the head of white clouds.
Previously, there was the Chan Master Baoyun of Xiong’er Mountain.
Although he resided at an ancient monastery, he did not maintain a single disciple.
When someone asked him, "Why does the Master not select a Dharma heir to carry on your lineage? he replied: [as recorded in the source].
Hai said,
"Zhilan has emerged in splendid brilliance, uniquely from Western Qin.
[The other] asked, "When will you arrive?"
Haikyo said,
"Your journey is finished;
the Master is about to arrive with his pack on his back."
The Abbot, Master Hai-ming, had his attendant strike the bell to assemble the community, saying,
"A disciple from the region west of the Pass has arrived.
Furthermore, this temple was originally founded by Guo Ziyi."
"Now the Abbot has come here in person;
you should go out to welcome him.
Just as the Master was entering the gate, [the Abbot arrived].
Seeing him from afar, Hai said,
"Why have you arrived so late, my lord?
The Master stepped forward and replied, "Yes."
Hǎi laughed heartily and ultimately conferred upon him the dharma robes, charging him to succeed to his seat;
he himself then withdrew into seclusion beside the temple.
Previously, there was a band of robbers who had settled there, plundering the people and causing them harm.
Someone requested that they be pursued by sea;
Hai replied:
"This is not within the capacity of an old monk like me.
Before long, Lord Guo will arrive and he will surely capture it himself.
The people did not understand his meaning.
After the Master had resided in the temple for only three days,
he led the assembly to capture them all and bind them;
they broke down their lair, intending to slaughter them all.
The bandits pleaded for their lives.
The Master spoke to them with composure, saying, "You have plundered wealth and taken human life; by the law of karma, you deserve death."
"Now that you beg for your life, do you not think of his life as well?
The bandit bowed his head until blood flowed, vowing to follow the precepts of the Triple Gem and never again commit evil.
The Master preached a verse for him, shaved his hair, and released him.
From that time on, for several decades, there were no items left unclaimed on the roads.
People began to believe that the Master was truly the reincarnation of Lord Guo.
In the twenty-fourth year of the Dading era of the Song dynasty, Master Hai passed away.
The Master was then serving as the abbot of Puzhao Monastery in Zhengzhou.
He later moved to Zhuge Hermitage in Sanxiang,
where he dressed in white robes, rode a yellow calf, and wandered through Luoyang blowing his short flute.
He once said:
"If you take me to be an ordinary person,
I have actually come from among the ranks of the sages."
If one says, "I am noble," one is still proceeding toward the state of an ordinary person. If one says,
"I am neither ordinary nor noble," [one is likewise proceeding toward the state of an ordinary person].
He then turned toward the summit of Vairocana, where there was yet another place for practice.
In the fifth year of the Taihe era, while observing the summer retreat at Dashi Temple in Lintao,
he expounded the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-śāstra* (The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment) and addressed the assembly, saying:
This assembly is nearly concluded;
I shall now depart.
On the evening of the twelfth day of the fifth month, I gave a small lecture for the community, discoursing upon the primary principle.
Rising at dawn, he called to his attendant monk, saying, "I am ill;
I shall go to seek medicine.
As the attendant was about to leave the door, [he said:]...
The Master had already passed away.
Above him, auspicious clouds of five colors swirled and coiled like a canopy;
a crimson radiance like that of the sun filled the four quarters, not dispersing for three days.
His worldly age was fifty-five,
and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇerī-vaṣa) was thirty-nine.
His disciples enshrined his entire body and erected a stūpa for him.
The commentary states:
When King Nala heard the music performed three times, Kāśyapa rose and danced three times;
if it were not due to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), whose would they be?
In the past, Guo Binyang was able to suppress rebels for the sake of the state and rescue the people from their plight;
now, having resided at Foguang Monastery for only three days, he has captured a band of thieves.
Is this not the result of his habitual tendencies?
Observing him dressed in white robes, riding a yellow calf, and playing the flute while wandering through Luoyang,
he claimed that there was a distinct place of practice atop the crown of Vairocana.
This, too, is truly inconceivable.
12. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xiaoying of Luhuo, Jiangxi. The Śramaṇa Shi Xiaoying of Luhuo, Jiangxi, whose courtesy name was Zhongwen, [was as follows].
His clan and lineage are unknown.
Having served in various monastic assemblies, he suddenly realized the Great Matter;
he was held in high esteem by the fourfold assembly.
Returning home late one evening to the banks of Lake Luo, he closed his gate and swept away visitors, refusing all contact with the world.

He devoted himself solely to what he had seen and heard throughout his life: the proclamations and teachings of venerable masters from various quarters, the religious discourses and debates shared by his friends, and whatever insights concerning the ancient canons and records he had gleaned from fragmentary inscriptions and moth-eaten scrolls.
All these have been compiled into a single volume titled *The Records of Layman Luohu*.

What is contained therein consists of the refined beauty of the words and deeds of world-renowned masters and virtuous scholars, as well as their sharp and swift spiritual flashes, their magnificent exchanges, and their vast and expansive spirit; these are sufficient to support the vehicle of the Dharma, instruct future students, and inspire people toward the ultimate good.
Therefore, readers could not bear to let go of the manuscript. 13.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Chanhui of Mount Ming Tianning Temple. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Chanhui of Mount Ming Tianning Temple, Number Thirteen. Shi Chanhui was a native of Mount Ming.
His family had followed the scholarly tradition for generations. Although he repeatedly took the imperial examinations, he did not achieve success.
During the Yuánfú era, the prefect Lǚ Yóuchéng mocked him by presenting him with a monk’s ordination certificate.
He subsequently abandoned Confucianism to follow the Buddhist teachings,
diligently studying the ancestral Way until he attained great enlightenment.
He first went forth to reside at Tianning Temple in his home district.
Whenever he went out or entered [his quarters], he invariably rode on horseback or in a carriage.
Several senior monks remarked that since the Buddha-dharma values ascetic practice, it was certainly inappropriate for him to ride in carriages or horses or wear fine silks and embroidery.
The Master replied with a verse:
Mañjuśrī rides a lion;
Samantabhadra mounts an elephant king.
It would do no harm for this newly arrived Buddha to ride a horse as well.
In all his preaching of the Dharma, his dialectical wit was swift and agile;
his recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulate in the world.

**Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Xiansong of the Xuanmi Yuan in Bachuan (14)** The Śramaṇa Shi Xiansong of the Xuanmi Yuan in Bachuan was a native of the Li family of Tóngliáng, Chóngqìng, Western Shǔ. He devoted himself to the purification of karma. [Text continues...]
Having completed his training and grown weary of worldly travel, he left the secular world to reside at Xuānmì Yuàn in Bāchuān.
For thirty years, he did not step beyond the threshold of his quarters.
During the Shàoxīng era, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:
For eighty years, he has been grandly opening his shop to trade in mani-jewels;
yet not a single person has come to deliberate with him.
It is not that this mountain monk closed his stall too early.
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
When his body was cremated, the śarīra relics were beyond counting.
At that time, there was the Venerable Jingye.
Shizhao was the son of the Wen family.
In his youth, he followed the occupation of a butcher.
He once had a sheep that was about to give birth to two lambs.
As he was about to kill them,
two lambs bit his knife and knelt prostrate at the door,
as if begging for their mother’s life.
The Master was moved with deep emotion and abandoned his home to become a monk.
He applied himself diligently to study under a master of the school and suddenly attained great enlightenment, composing a verse that said:
"Yesterday I had the mind of a rākṣasa."
This morning I beheld the face of the Bodhisattva;
the rākṣasa and the Bodhisattva were not separated by so much as a single thread.

15. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Faquan of Jingji in Pingjiang Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Faquan of Jingji in Pingjiang, Number Fifteen. Shi Faquan, whose courtesy name was Wuan, was a native of Changzhou in Wu. His ancestors were of the Liu clan. His great-great-grandfather, Liu Sheng, served as the Governor of Xuzhou during the Jin dynasty. His grandfather, Liu Zhi, served as the Magistrate of Dongyang during the Song dynasty. His father, Liu Xian, served as the Magistrate of Xunyang during the Yuan dynasty. Faquan was born in the year of the Jiazi cycle (1264) during the Dade era of the Yuan dynasty. From his youth, he possessed a sharp and clear intellect; he was naturally inclined toward the Way and had no desire for worldly affairs. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order under the Venerable Zongxiao at the Huayan Monastery in Suzhou. He studied the Vinaya and the Abhidharma with great diligence. Later, he traveled to Mount Tiantai to receive full ordination from the Venerable Zhixiang. Subsequently, he visited various eminent masters throughout the land to inquire about the profound mysteries of the teachings. He then returned to Mount Tiantai to serve the Venerable Zhixiang as his attendant. Zhixiang was a direct successor to the Dharma of the Great Master Zhenxie Qingliao. Faquan served him for many years, receiving instruction in both the exoteric and esoteric teachings. Zhixiang frequently praised him, saying, "This child possesses the capacity to carry on our lineage. In the year of the Bingwu cycle (1306), he received the imperial decree to reside at the Jingci Monastery in Lin'an. He subsequently traveled to the Eastern Capital (Nanjing) to visit the Chan Master Daoyan at the Tianping Monastery. Daoyan was a Dharma heir of the Chan Master Wuxin of Mount Jing. Faquan studied under him for several years, attaining deep realization. He then returned to Mount Tiantai and took up residence at the Fayun Monastery. Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi Daochong of Jing Mountain in Lin’an. The Śramaṇa Shi Daochong of Jing Mountain in Lin’an, number sixteen: Shi Daochong, whose style name was Chijue (Ultimate Folly).
Wuxin Changjiang was the son of Lady Xun.
He first attended Master Caoyuan Sheng of Miaoguo Temple in Hangzhou, where he attained great enlightenment regarding the profound essence of the Dharma.
He subsequently emerged into the world at Tianning Temple in Jiahe.
He subsequently moved to Mount Jiangshan Xuefeng.
Not long after, he received an imperial decree to reside at Tiantong in Mingzhou for three years;
thereafter, by imperial edict, he was appointed to Lingyin.
At that time, the Prefect of Jingzhao was constructing Fahua Temple and specially submitted a petition requesting the Master to serve as its first patriarch.
The request was granted, yet he did not go.
Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree appointing him as the abbot of Shuangjing Monastery in Hangzhou.
The Master said to the assembly,
"If I do not go to Fahua [Monastery], you will not believe me."
To disobey the command of Mount Jing would be a lack of reverence;
having already lost both reverence and trustworthiness,
how could one serve as a model for later students?
He then indolently proceeded to the Dharma Hall of Fahua Monastery;
after more than a month, he received the imperial decree to ascend Mount Jing,
whereupon the entire assembly responded in unison with a roar of joy like thunder.
As he approached the time of his passing, he personally recorded in writing the account of how he had attained the Dharma.
He ascended the hall to preach the Dharma and bid farewell to the assembly;
then, entering his quarters, he gave instructions regarding his final affairs.
At nightfall, while sitting upright and discussing the Way with the assembly for some time, he passed away peacefully.
This was on the fifteenth day of the third month in the third year of the Lizong era.
He was eighty-two years of age at the time of his death.
His monastic seniority was sixty-one years.
Upon cremation, his relics were brilliantly radiant;
his disciples divided them between two stupas.
One was at Yuzhi Hermitage in the Shanpu Fields of his native mountain;
the other was at Yushan Hermitage in Jinling. 17.
Biography of the Śramaṇa Shi De-fu of Xingsheng Temple in Baoding. The seventeenth, Shi De-fu, was the son of the Xie family of Yi County in Baoding.
At the age of seven, he earnestly sought to leave the household life.
His parents, moved by a miraculous dream, eventually allowed him to enter Xingxing Temple.
There, under the guidance of Master Zhenkong, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He diligently investigated the Great Dharma.
One day, while engaged in walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
From that time on, his fame spread throughout the monastic community.

At the beginning of the Huangqing era of the Song dynasty, the Venerable Wanshan Shou, by imperial decree, was extensively promoting the Water and Land (Shuilu) feast assemblies and invited the Master to ascend the hall and preach the Dharma.
The seven classes of disciples gathered in full assembly.
Just as the Master was ascending the seat to recite a verse, [the Emperor arrived].
Suddenly, while seated, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the reaches of space and manifested various auspicious signs.
After a long while, the light vanished; subsequently, the imperial court bestowed upon him the title "Great Master Tongbian" (Master of Universal Eloquence) along with a golden *saṃghāṭī* robe.
When he later manifested his parinirvāṇa, a white light emerged from the crown of his head, illuminating the four directions.
Upon cremation, several dozen śarīras were obtained,
for which a stūpa was erected.
The Biographies of Eminent Monks Compiled in the Great Ming, Volume Eight, End.
